META.subject: Core Mathematics
META.subtitleDoc: CBE Phenomenon-Driven Lesson Sequence — Sub-Strand 2.9 (8 Lessons)

UNIT.subject: Core Mathematics
UNIT.content:
• Distance, displacement, speed, velocity, and acceleration — definitions, units, and real-life meaning
• Velocity and acceleration — calculating velocity and acceleration from given data
• Displacement-time graph — drawing displacement-time graphs from tables of values
• Interpretation of displacement-time graph — extracting velocity, rest periods, and direction from the graph
• Velocity-time graph — drawing velocity-time graphs from tables of values
• Interpretation of velocity-time graph — extracting acceleration, distance travelled, and deceleration from the graph
• Relative speed — calculating relative speed of two bodies moving in the same or opposite directions
• Application of linear motion — solving real-life problems involving linear motion concepts
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) explain the terms distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration in real-life situations,
b) determine velocity and acceleration in different situations,
c) draw a displacement-time graph of different situations,
d) interpret displacement-time graph in different situations,
e) draw a velocity-time graph from given tables in different situations,
f) interpret velocity-time graph in different situations,
g) determine relative speed of two moving bodies in different situations,
h) appreciate use of linear motion in real-life situations.
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Communication and Collaboration: the learner discusses different displacement-time graphs with peers, presents findings from races and motion experiments, and collaborates to interpret velocity-time graphs in group activities.
• Self-Efficacy: the learner participates in a race of a specified distance on the school field, records the time taken by each learner, and confidently works out the velocity and acceleration of different learners.
• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: the learner observes two bodies in motion — such as matatus when overtaking on Thika Road or Mombasa Road — and works out the relative speed of the two vehicles, reasoning about the dangers of careless overtaking.
UNIT.values:
• Responsibility: as the learner uses objects in motion such as thrown balls, rolling carts, or running peers to explain distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration, and takes care of measuring equipment such as stopwatches and tape measures.
• Integrity: as the learner participates in a race of a specified distance, records time taken by each learner honestly, and accurately works out the velocity and acceleration of different learners without falsifying results.
• Unity: as the learner participates and collaborates in group races and data-recording exercises to record time taken by each learner and work out the velocity and acceleration of different learners.
UNIT.sep:
• Analysing and Interpreting Data: the learner collects time and distance data from a school running race or a rolling object, plots displacement-time and velocity-time graphs, and draws conclusions about motion patterns from the shape of the graphs.
• Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking: the learner applies formulas for velocity (v = s/t) and acceleration (a = Δv/Δt), calculates areas under velocity-time graphs to find distance, and computes gradients of displacement-time graphs to find speed.
• Constructing Explanations: the learner uses evidence from graphs and calculations to explain the motion of matatus, cyclists in the Tour du Rwanda, or athletes at the Nairobi Marathon, connecting mathematical results to real-world behaviour.
• Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information: the learner presents motion data collected during the school race to the class, evaluates the accuracy of readings, and communicates findings using correctly labelled graphs and written interpretations.
UNIT.pcis:
• Learner Support Programmes (Sports and Games): the learner participates in a race of a specified distance on the school field, records time taken by each learner and works out the velocity and acceleration — connecting mathematics to athletics and physical education.
• Socio-Economic and Environmental Issues (Safety and Security): the learner observes two bodies in motion such as matatus when overtaking or moving in opposite directions along Kenyan highways and works out the relative speed of these two bodies in motion, appreciating the mathematical basis of road safety regulations.
• Road Safety: as the learner observes two vehicles when one is overtaking, discusses and works out the relative speed of the two vehicles, and also discusses the dangers of careless overtaking on Kenyan roads such as the Nairobi–Nakuru highway.
UNIT.careers:
• Traffic Engineering and Road Safety: understanding velocity, acceleration, and relative speed underpins the design of speed limits, safe overtaking zones, and traffic light timing on Kenyan roads managed by KENHA and NTSA.
• Athletics Coaching and Sports Science: coaches at Athletics Kenya use displacement-time and velocity-time data to analyse sprint performance, pace strategy, and acceleration profiles of athletes like Faith Kipyegon and Eliud Kipchoge.
• Aviation and Railway Transport: Kenya Airways pilots and SGR (Standard Gauge Railway) operators use principles of linear motion — including velocity, acceleration, and braking distance — to plan safe operations.
• Physics and Engineering: a foundation in linear motion kinematics is essential for university-level physics and mechanical engineering programmes at institutions such as the University of Nairobi and Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology (JKUAT).
• Logistics and Supply Chain: fleet managers at companies operating along the Northern Corridor (Mombasa–Nairobi–Kampala) use speed, distance, and time calculations to plan delivery schedules and fuel efficiency.
UNIT.focus: This unit develops learners' ability to describe, calculate, graphically represent, and interpret linear motion using the key quantities of distance, displacement, speed, velocity, acceleration, and relative speed. Learners move from concrete experience — running a measured race on the school field and timing each other with stopwatches — through graphical modelling on displacement-time and velocity-time graphs, to abstract problem-solving involving relative speed of vehicles on Kenyan highways. Throughout the unit, Kenyan contexts such as the Nairobi Marathon, SGR train journeys, matatu overtaking on the Nakuru–Nairobi highway, and athletes at Kipchoge Keino Stadium anchor every mathematical concept in meaningful real-life experience.
UNIT.phenomenon: A VIDEO CLIP AND DATA PRINTOUT of the 2023 Nairobi Marathon is shown to the class. The clip shows elite runners — including Kenyan athletes — accelerating off the start line, settling into a steady pace along Uhuru Highway, slowing slightly at water stations, and sprinting to the finish. Alongside the clip, a printed table shows the split times (time recorded at every 5 km mark) for two runners: Runner A (who runs at a nearly constant pace) and Runner B (who starts fast, slows in the middle, and sprints at the end). Students are asked: "Both runners finished the 42 km race, but their split-time tables look completely different — Runner B was actually ahead at 30 km but Runner A won. How can we use numbers and graphs to explain exactly what happened at every point in the race?" This is puzzling because students intuitively know both runners covered the same distance, yet the patterns of their motion were completely different — and a simple calculation of total time does not reveal the story of acceleration, varying velocity, and the critical sprint finish. Students must grapple with the difference between average speed and instantaneous velocity, and with how the shape of a graph — not just its start and end points — tells the full story of motion.
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• A STOPWATCH DATA SHEET from a 100 m sprint on the school field: learners race in groups of four over a measured 100 m track; a timekeeper records the time at 25 m, 50 m, 75 m, and 100 m for each runner. Learners notice that the time gaps between checkpoints are not equal — the runner did not cover each 25 m segment in the same time — raising the question of how velocity changes during the race.
• AN SGR TIMETABLE AND ROUTE MAP: the Standard Gauge Railway Madaraka Express departs Nairobi (Syokimau) at 08:00 and arrives in Mombasa at 12:30, covering approximately 480 km. Learners examine the published stop times at Emali, Kibwezi, Mtito Andei, and Voi and notice the train spends different amounts of time between stations — connecting real timetable data to the concept of varying velocity and distance-time relationships.
• A DASH-CAM VIDEO DESCRIPTION of a matatu overtaking a lorry on the Nairobi–Nakuru highway: the matatu travels at 120 km/h and the lorry at 80 km/h in the same direction. Learners discuss how fast the matatu appears to be moving relative to the lorry — introducing the concept of relative speed — and connect this to the dangers of overtaking, as regulated by NTSA Kenya.
• A STROBE PHOTOGRAPH (or printed simulation) of a ball rolling down a ramp at Mwalimu Kariuki's physics lab: equally-spaced time intervals produce unequally-spaced position marks, showing that the ball is accelerating. Students find it puzzling that equal time steps produce unequal distances — setting up the distinction between constant speed and acceleration.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: How can we use mathematics — calculations and graphs — to fully describe and explain the motion of any moving body, from a Nairobi Marathon runner to a matatu on the Nakuru highway?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTIONS:
1. What is speed?
2. How do we use displacement-time graphs in real life?
3. How do we use velocity-time graphs?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1 — Anchoring Phenomenon & Key Terms: Learners watch the Nairobi Marathon video clip and examine the split-time data for Runner A and Runner B. Through guided discussion, learners define and distinguish distance vs. displacement, speed vs. velocity, and are introduced to acceleration. They complete a class race on the school field (or corridor) using stopwatches and tape measures, recording their own distance-time data. The driving question is posted on the Driving Question Board (DQB).

Lesson 2 — Calculating Velocity and Acceleration: Using data from the school race and the SGR timetable supporting phenomenon, learners practise calculating velocity (v = s/t) and acceleration (a = Δv/Δt) in different situations — uniform and non-uniform motion. Worked examples use Kenyan contexts: Kipchoge's marathon pace, a boda-boda accelerating from rest. Learners update the DQB with new understanding of "what speed actually means mathematically."

Lesson 3 — Drawing Displacement-Time Graphs: Learners use their own school-race data and the marathon split-time table to plot displacement-time graphs on squared paper. They learn conventions (labelled axes, title, correct units) and distinguish between graphs showing constant speed (straight line), rest (horizontal line), and return journey (downward slope). Learners predict what Runner B's graph will look like before plotting it.

Lesson 4 — Interpreting Displacement-Time Graphs: Learners interpret a set of pre-drawn displacement-time graphs representing different real-life scenarios: a matatu stopping at a stage, a runner resting, a cyclist returning home. They calculate the gradient of each segment and connect gradient to velocity. The SGR stop-data is used to interpret a multi-segment graph. Learners revise their DQB entries — now able to answer "How do we use displacement-time graphs in real life?"

Lesson 5 — Drawing Velocity-Time Graphs: Learners are introduced to velocity-time graphs using the ball-on-a-ramp supporting phenomenon and marathon sprint-finish data. They construct velocity-time graphs from given tables of values for scenarios such as a matatu accelerating from a bus stop, cruising at constant speed, and braking. Learners identify the gradient (acceleration) and the shape of each segment.

Lesson 6 — Interpreting Velocity-Time Graphs: Learners interpret velocity-time graphs to extract acceleration, deceleration, and total distance travelled (area under the graph — counting squares and using trapezium/rectangle area). Real-life graphs include an SGR train journey and a 400 m school race. Learners connect area under the graph back to displacement, answering why Runner B lost despite leading at 30 km. The DQB is updated to address "How do we use velocity-time graphs?"

Lesson 7 — Relative Speed: Using the matatu-overtaking supporting phenomenon, learners explore relative speed of two bodies moving in the same direction (relative speed = difference) and in opposite directions (relative speed = sum). They solve problems involving vehicles on Kenyan highways, boats on Lake Victoria, and runners passing each other on a track. Road safety implications of high relative speed are discussed and connected to NTSA speed limits.

Lesson 8 — Consolidation, Model Building & Assessment: Learners return to the original Nairobi Marathon data and now produce a complete mathematical explanation of Runner A vs. Runner B — including calculations, a displacement-time graph, a velocity-time graph, and a written interpretation of the sprint finish. They present their models to the class, updating the DQB with final answers to all three KICD key inquiry questions. A class written assessment covers all sub-strand outcomes. Learners reflect on careers that use linear motion mathematics.

LESSONS.title: Anchoring Phenomenon & Key Terms: What Is Really Happening in the Nairobi Marathon?

slo.purpose: To anchor learners in the driving question by introducing the Nairobi Marathon phenomenon, establishing the key vocabulary of linear motion (distance, displacement, speed, velocity, acceleration), and collecting first-hand motion data through a class race activity.
slo.knowledge: Learners explain the terms distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration in real-life situations. (KICD SLO 2.9a)
slo.skills: Learners participate in a measured race, record distance-time data using stopwatches and tape measures, and calculate average speed from their own results. Learners begin to distinguish between scalar and vector quantities with examples drawn from the marathon context. (KICD SLO 2.9b — introductory; KICD Core Competency: Self-Efficacy)
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate that mathematics is a precise language for describing motion, value integrity in recording accurate data, and demonstrate unity by collaborating during the class race. (KICD Values: Integrity, Unity, Responsibility)
slo.keyInquiry: What is speed? (KICD Key Inquiry Question 1, Sub-Strand 2.9)
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is Lesson 1 of the Linear Motion unit — the opening lesson that launches the anchoring phenomenon. Learners encounter the puzzle of Runner A vs. Runner B in the 2023 Nairobi Marathon split-time data, experience motion first-hand in a school-field race, and post the driving question on the Driving Question Board (DQB). Every subsequent lesson will return to this phenomenon to deepen understanding.
slo.safetyNotes: During the class race on the school field or corridor: (1) Ensure the running surface is clear of stones, wet patches, and obstacles before the activity. (2) Learners with physical limitations may serve as timekeepers or data recorders — include all learners meaningfully. (3) Remind learners to warm up briefly (10 seconds of jogging on the spot) before the sprint to reduce injury risk. (4) No pushing or overtaking dangerously — this reinforces the road-safety PCI on safe overtaking discussed in the lesson.

LESSONS.overview: Learners watch a short video clip of the 2023 Nairobi Marathon showing Kenyan elite runners accelerating off the start line on Uhuru Highway, settling into a steady pace, slowing at water stations, and sprinting to the finish. They examine a printed split-time table for Runner A (nearly constant pace) and Runner B (fast start, mid-race slowdown, sprint finish) and grapple with the puzzle: both covered 42 km, yet Runner A won even though Runner B was ahead at 30 km. Through guided discussion learners define and distinguish distance vs. displacement, speed vs. velocity, and are introduced to the concept of acceleration. They then conduct a class race on the school field — measured distances of 40 m and 80 m — recording their own time data with stopwatches and calculating average speed. The lesson closes by posting the driving question on the Driving Question Board and capturing learners' first questions and wonderings.

framework.phase: Phase 1 — PREDICT: What Do You Already Think Is Happening?
framework.learnerExperience: Learners receive the printed split-time data table for Runner A and Runner B (time recorded at every 5 km mark for the full 42 km Nairobi Marathon). Working individually for 3 minutes, they study the table silently and write answers to two prompts in their exercise books: (1) 'Using only the numbers in this table, who do you think is the faster runner — and why?' (2) 'At what point in the race did the situation change between the two runners?' Learners then share predictions with a shoulder partner for 2 minutes before a whole-class share-out. No answer is marked right or wrong at this stage — all predictions are recorded on the chalkboard under the heading 'OUR PREDICTIONS'.
framework.teacherMoves: BEFORE CLASS: Print one split-time data sheet per learner (or pair). Write the two prediction prompts on the chalkboard. Cue the marathon video clip to the start. | LAUNCH (0–3 min): Distribute the data sheet. Say exactly: 'Do not talk yet. Read this table quietly for three minutes. Use your pencil to circle anything that surprises you.' Set a visible timer. | INDIVIDUAL THINK TIME: Allow 3 minutes of silent reading. Circulate and scan for misconceptions — look for learners who confuse 'split time' with 'total time'. | PAIR SHARE (3–6 min): Say: 'Now turn to your neighbour. You have two minutes. Compare your circles and agree on one answer to each prompt.' | WHOLE-CLASS COLD-CALL (6–10 min): Cold-call at least 5 different learners using name cards or random selection. Ask: 'Amina, what did you predict — and what number in the table made you say that?' WAIT 12 SECONDS after each name before prompting. Record every prediction verbatim on the board — do NOT evaluate yet. After 5 responses, say: 'Hold these predictions. We are about to watch what actually happened.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction Protocol — Activating Prior Knowledge: By committing predictions to paper before instruction, learners surface their intuitive understanding of speed and motion. This creates cognitive dissonance when the video reveals that Runner B — who looked faster in the first half — lost the race. That dissonance is the engine that drives inquiry throughout the unit.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Can learners identify which 5 km split shows Runner B's slowdown (km 25–35) and which shows Runner A's consistency? Circulate during individual think time and note the exercise books of 3–4 learners who appear stuck — these learners may need scaffolding in Phase 2. Do not correct at this stage; note for follow-up.

framework.phase: Phase 2 — OBSERVE: The Marathon Video Clip & Data Examination
framework.learnerExperience: The teacher plays the 2023 Nairobi Marathon video clip (3–5 minutes) showing: the mass start on Uhuru Highway, elite Kenyan runners including pacemakers settling into rhythm along Kenyatta Avenue, the visible slowdown at a water station near the 30 km mark, and the sprint finish. While watching, learners use a simple three-column observation table in their books: 'What I SEE happening to the runner's motion | What it MEANS about their speed | My QUESTION.' After the clip, learners spend 4 minutes completing their observation tables. The teacher then hands out (or projects) a colour-coded version of the split-time table with Runner A in blue and Runner B in red, and guides learners through reading the table row by row using a 'Notice and Wonder' protocol. Key data points highlighted: Runner B's 0–5 km split is 16 min (very fast); Runner A's 0–5 km split is 18 min (steady). At 30 km, Runner B is ahead by 4 minutes total. By 42 km, Runner A wins by 2 minutes.
framework.teacherMoves: VIDEO SCREENING (10–16 min): Dim lights if possible. Say: 'As you watch, fill in column one of your observation table — just describe the motion you see. You will fill columns two and three after.' Play the clip without pausing. | POST-VIDEO WRITING (16–20 min): Say: 'Now, in silence, complete all three columns. You have four minutes.' Circulate. Look for learners who write 'Runner B slows down' — these are ready for the vocabulary upgrade in Phase 3. | GUIDED TABLE READING (20–28 min): Project or draw the split-time table on the board. Point to the 30 km row. Say: 'At this exact moment in the race, Runner B is ahead. Raise your hand if your prediction said Runner B would win.' (Count hands aloud — e.g., 'I see 14 hands.') Then point to the 42 km row. Say: 'But here is the finish. Runner A won. Spend 30 seconds — look at the numbers between row 30 km and row 42 km. What changed?' WAIT 30 SECONDS. Cold-call 3 learners: 'Kipchoge, what number jumped out at you?' | TRANSITION QUESTION (28–30 min): Say: 'We can see something changed — but the table only gives us total split times. It does not tell us exactly how fast each runner was going at each moment. That is the problem mathematics helps us solve. That is why we are here.' Write on the board: 'HOW CAN NUMBERS AND GRAPHS TELL THE FULL STORY OF MOTION?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Notice and Wonder with Structured Observation Table — Evidence-Based Sensemaking: The three-column table (See / Means / Question) trains learners to separate raw observation from interpretation, which is NGSS Science & Engineering Practice 4 (Analysing and Interpreting Data). By labelling what the motion 'means' before they have the vocabulary, learners construct their own proto-definitions of speed and acceleration, which the teacher can then formalise in Phase 3.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: In the 'Means' column, can learners use comparative language — 'Runner B is moving faster at the start', 'Runner A barely changes speed'? Collect 5–6 books during the 4-minute writing period and photograph the observation tables for later review. Flag learners who leave the 'Means' column blank — they may need a language scaffold (sentence starter: 'This means the runner is moving _____ than before').

framework.phase: Phase 3 — EXPLAIN: Defining the Language of Motion
framework.learnerExperience: Using the marathon context as the reference throughout, the teacher guides learners through a whole-class concept-building discussion to define, distinguish, and record five key terms: distance, displacement, speed, velocity, and acceleration. Learners create a 'Vocabulary Anchor Chart' in their books — a two-column table with the term and a marathon-based example they write themselves. Key distinctions built: (a) Distance (scalar) = total path covered, e.g., Runner A ran 42 km of road. Displacement (vector) = straight-line change in position with direction, e.g., the Nairobi Marathon start and finish are both on Uhuru Highway, so displacement ≠ 42 km. (b) Speed (scalar) = distance ÷ time, e.g., Runner A's average speed over the race. Velocity (vector) = displacement ÷ time with direction. (c) Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time, e.g., Runner B accelerated in the final 2 km sprint. Learners then conduct a rapid calculation: using Runner A's total time (approx. 2 hr 12 min = 132 min) and the distance 42 km, they calculate Runner A's average speed in km/min and km/h. This is the first mathematical computation of the unit.
framework.teacherMoves: VOCABULARY BUILD (30–48 min): Draw a two-column table on the board: 'TERM | MARATHON EXAMPLE'. Do NOT pre-fill it. For each term: (1) Ask learners to attempt a definition from the video/table evidence. (2) WAIT 12 SECONDS. (3) Cold-call 2 learners per term. (4) Refine the definition collaboratively and write it. Say for distance vs. displacement: 'The marathon route runs from the Kenya National Theatre along Uhuru Highway and loops back. Runner A ran 42 km of road. But is the start point and the finish point the same place? Kimani, what do you think the displacement is?' WAIT 12 SECONDS. Guide to the idea that if start = finish (loop), displacement = 0. Say: 'This is why direction matters in mathematics.' | CALCULATION TASK (48–55 min): Write on the board: 'Runner A finishes in 2 hours 12 minutes. The race is 42 km. Calculate Runner A's average speed.' Say: 'Work individually. You have 4 minutes. Show every step.' After 4 minutes, cold-call one learner to come to the board and work through the solution. Affirm correct method: Speed = Distance ÷ Time = 42 ÷ 2.2 = 19.09 km/h (approx.). Say: 'This is the average. But is Runner A always moving at exactly 19 km/h? Fatuma, look at the split-time table — what does it tell you?' WAIT 12 SECONDS. Draw out the concept of varying speed leading to the need for graphs. | CONNECT TO PHENOMENON: Say: 'We now have the words. In the next lessons we will build the graphs that show the full story — not just the average, but every moment of the race.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Co-Constructed Vocabulary Anchor Chart — Language for Thinking: Rather than lecturing definitions, the teacher elicits proto-definitions from learners' own observations and refines them collaboratively. This is NGSS Practice 6 (Constructing Explanations). Every definition is anchored to a specific moment in the marathon video or split-time table, so vocabulary is never abstract. The first calculation task (average speed) simultaneously activates numeracy skills and reveals the limitation of averages — creating the motivation for graphs in later lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Can learners correctly distinguish the scalar/vector pairs in a quick oral check? After filling the anchor chart, pose this rapid-fire question to the whole class (hands-down, cold-call): 'Achieng — if a matatu in Nairobi travels 10 km east and then 10 km west back to the start, what is the distance? What is the displacement?' Correct answer: distance = 20 km; displacement = 0 km. If more than one-third of cold-called learners (target: call 4) confuse these, pause and use a number line drawn on the board to re-teach before the field activity.

framework.phase: Phase 4 — DRIVING QUESTION BOARD (DQB): Capturing Our Wonderings
framework.learnerExperience: After returning from the field activity (which runs concurrently with or immediately after Phase 3 — see teacher moves), the class gathers to formally post the Driving Question Board. Each learner receives two sticky notes (or torn pieces of paper). On the FIRST sticky note they write one thing they now know or understand about motion. On the SECOND sticky note they write one question they still have — something the marathon data or field race made them wonder about. Sticky notes are posted on the DQB (a dedicated section of the chalkboard or a large sheet of manila paper). The teacher reads out 5–6 questions aloud and groups them into clusters: 'Questions about graphs', 'Questions about the difference between speed and velocity', 'Questions about acceleration'. The driving question is written in large letters at the top of the DQB: 'HOW CAN WE USE MATHEMATICS — CALCULATIONS AND GRAPHS — TO FULLY DESCRIBE AND EXPLAIN THE MOTION OF ANY MOVING BODY, FROM A NAIROBI MARATHON RUNNER TO A MATATU ON THE NAKURU HIGHWAY?'
framework.teacherMoves: DQB SETUP (55–65 min): Before this phase, prepare the DQB space on the board. Distribute two sticky notes (or paper squares) per learner. Say: 'You have three minutes. On the YELLOW note, write one thing you now understand. On the GREEN note, write one question you still have. Be specific — use the marathon or the race we just ran as your example.' WAIT 3 MINUTES of silent writing. | POSTING (65–68 min): Invite all learners to post their notes simultaneously. Quickly scan the board. Read 5–6 questions aloud, paraphrasing where needed: 'Mutua asks: why did Runner B slow down — is that acceleration?' 'Zawadi asks: how do we draw a graph from the split times?' Say: 'These are exactly the questions we will answer in this unit. Every lesson, we will come back to this board and move questions from the question side to the answer side.' | DRIVING QUESTION POSTING (68–70 min): Write or unveil the pre-prepared driving question banner. Read it aloud twice — once yourself, once with the class chorally. Say: 'This is our mission for the next several lessons. Keep it in mind.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board — Making Thinking Visible: The DQB is a living artefact that externalises the class's evolving understanding. By separating 'what I know' from 'what I wonder', learners practise metacognition (NGSS Practice 1: Asking Questions). Clustering questions into themes previews the unit structure and gives learners agency — their own questions drive the curriculum forward.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Are learners' 'know' sticky notes conceptually accurate (e.g., 'Speed = distance ÷ time') rather than trivially descriptive (e.g., 'Runners run fast')? Are 'wonder' sticky notes genuinely inquiry-oriented (e.g., 'How does the graph look when a runner speeds up suddenly?') rather than off-topic? Photograph the DQB at the end of class. Count: (a) number of questions related to graphs — this gauges readiness for Lessons 2–3; (b) number of questions that conflate speed and velocity — target these explicitly in Lesson 2.

framework.phase: Phase 5 — MODEL BUILDING: Our First Motion Model — The Class Race Data Table
framework.learnerExperience: Learners conduct a class race on the school field (or a marked corridor) as their first evidence-gathering model-building activity. The class is organised into groups of 6–8. Each group marks out a 40 m course using a tape measure (two cones or chalk marks). Within each group: 2 learners run (one at a time), 2 learners operate stopwatches (timing at 10 m, 20 m, 30 m, 40 m intervals marked with chalk), 2 learners record data in a shared table, and remaining learners observe and note qualitative descriptions ('accelerating at the start', 'steady in the middle', 'tiring at the end'). Every learner runs at least once. Data collected per runner: time at 10 m, 20 m, 30 m, 40 m. Back in class, each learner copies their group's data table into their exercise book and calculates average speed for each 10 m interval. They label each interval as 'accelerating', 'steady', or 'decelerating' based on whether speed increased, stayed similar, or decreased. This table is explicitly labelled 'MY FIRST MOTION MODEL — [Date]' and will be revised and expanded as a graph in Lesson 2.
framework.teacherMoves: FIELD SETUP (run during or immediately after Phase 3, approximately 35–50 min mark, adjust to school timetable): Before the lesson, mark the 40 m course on the field with chalk at 10 m intervals. Prepare a data recording template on the board (or as a printed handout): Runner Name | Time at 10 m | Time at 20 m | Time at 30 m | Time at 40 m | Average Speed (each interval). | BRIEFING (2 min): Say: 'We are going to do what the Nairobi Marathon organisers did — collect our own split-time data. Your job is to record the time at every 10 m mark, just like the marathon recorders at every 5 km. We will use this data in the next lesson to draw our first graph.' Assign roles clearly. Demonstrate stopwatch use. | RACE ACTIVITY (15 min on field): Circulate between groups. Check that timers start at the runner's first movement (not the command). Prompt data recorders: 'Write the time the moment the runner crosses the chalk line — not when you think they crossed it. Accuracy matters.' For groups with inconsistent data, ask: 'Is your average speed for interval 3 higher or lower than interval 1? What does that tell you about how your runner was moving?' | DATA ANALYSIS BACK IN CLASS (50–55 min, overlaps with Phase 3 close): Say: 'Calculate the average speed for each 10 m interval using Speed = Distance ÷ Time. Then label each interval. Use the words from our vocabulary chart.' WAIT for individual work (4 min). Cold-call 2 learners to share their most interesting finding. Ask: 'Odhiambo, did your runner's speed change from interval 1 to interval 4? What does that remind you of in the marathon data?' | MODEL LABELLING: Say: 'Write at the top of this table: MY FIRST MOTION MODEL. In Lesson 2, we will turn this table into a graph — just like the kind of graph that could explain the marathon.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: First-Person Data Collection as Model Building — NGSS Practice 3 (Planning and Carrying Out Investigations) & Practice 5 (Using Mathematics): By generating their own split-time data, learners experience the same data-collection challenge as marathon race organisers. Labelling each interval as 'accelerating / steady / decelerating' is a proto-model of motion — a precursor to the displacement-time and velocity-time graphs in Lessons 2–4. Explicitly titling the table 'MY FIRST MOTION MODEL' establishes the unit-long practice of iterative model revision, directly mirroring NGSS Practice 2 (Developing and Using Models).
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Can learners correctly compute speed = distance ÷ time for each 10 m interval and use the comparative values to correctly label the interval as accelerating, steady, or decelerating? Exit check — before learners leave, pose this verbal question (whole class, hands up): 'If your speed in interval 1 is 4.2 m/s and your speed in interval 2 is 5.1 m/s, are you accelerating or decelerating?' Target: at least 80% of learners respond correctly. If not, clarify before dismissal: 'Acceleration means speed is INCREASING. The number gets BIGGER. In Lesson 2 we will see this as the slope of a graph.'

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following questions and record brief notes: (1) PHENOMENON ENGAGEMENT — Did the marathon split-time data create genuine puzzlement? Did learners spontaneously ask 'why' questions, or did they remain passive? If passive, consider adding a more dramatic data point (e.g., Runner B's pace at km 35 compared to km 5) to sharpen the anomaly in Lesson 1 of the next class cycle. (2) VOCABULARY GAPS — Which of the five key terms (distance, displacement, speed, velocity, acceleration) caused the most confusion? Displacement is typically the hardest for Grade 10 learners because it requires directional thinking. If more than one-third of cold-called learners confused distance and displacement, plan a 5-minute warm-up activity at the start of Lesson 2 using a number line drawn on the school field. (3) FIELD ACTIVITY LOGISTICS — Did groups collect clean, reliable data? If stopwatch errors produced obviously incorrect splits (e.g., a 10 m split faster than a world record), use these as a teaching moment in Lesson 2: 'Why might our data be unreliable? What would a scientist do?' (4) DQB QUALITY — Review the photographed sticky notes. Are learners' questions specific enough to drive the next lesson? If questions are very generic ('I wonder about speed'), prompt more specific questions at the start of Lesson 2 by modelling: 'A better question might be — what does the shape of a graph look like when Runner B is accelerating in the final 2 km?' (5) INCLUSION CHECK — Were all learners — including those with physical limitations who served as timekeepers — genuinely included in the data collection and sensemaking? Adjust roles in the next practical activity if needed.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Watched the 2023 Nairobi Marathon video clip showing Kenyan elite runners accelerating off the start on Uhuru Highway, running at a steady pace, slowing at water stations, and sprinting to the finish. Examined the split-time table for Runner A (consistent pace) and Runner B (fast start, mid-race slowdown, strong sprint) and noticed that Runner B was ahead at 30 km but Runner A won. Conducted a class race on the school field, recording our own split times at 10 m intervals using stopwatches and tape measures.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Distance is the total path length covered (a scalar quantity — no direction needed). Displacement is the straight-line change in position from start to finish, including direction (a vector quantity). Speed = distance ÷ time (scalar). Velocity = displacement ÷ time with direction (vector). Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity — it explains why Runner B's split times changed dramatically between 30 km and 42 km. We calculated Runner A's average speed as approximately 19 km/h, and we calculated our own average speed over each 10 m interval of the class race.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Runner A won the 2023 Nairobi Marathon even though Runner B was ahead at 30 km because Runner B's velocity decreased sharply in the middle kilometres while Runner A maintained a nearly constant velocity throughout. Runner B's sprint in the final 2 km was not enough to overcome the time lost. A single average speed calculation cannot reveal this — we need a graph that shows what is happening at every moment of the race. Our class race data table is our first motion model, and in the next lesson we will convert it into a displacement-time graph to see the full story of motion.
