LESSONS.title: Calculating Velocity and Acceleration — Making the Numbers Tell the Story
LESSONS.aresKeywords: velocity calculation, acceleration formula, uniform motion, non-uniform motion, linear motion Kenya

slo.purpose: Learners move from naming the concepts of velocity and acceleration (Lesson 1) to calculating them precisely using v = s/t and a = Δv/Δt, applying these formulas to split-time data from the Nairobi Marathon and other Kenyan motion contexts.
slo.knowledge:
• Define velocity as the rate of change of displacement with time (v = s/t) and state its SI unit (m/s or km/h)
• Define acceleration as the rate of change of velocity with time (a = Δv/Δt) and state its SI unit (m/s²)
• Distinguish between uniform motion (constant velocity, zero acceleration) and non-uniform motion (changing velocity, non-zero acceleration)
slo.skills:
• Calculate velocity and acceleration from given displacement, speed, and time data in different real-life situations
• Identify and interpret intervals of uniform and non-uniform motion from a table of split-time data
slo.attitudes:
• Appreciate that mathematical precision — not intuition alone — is needed to fully describe motion and explain outcomes like a marathon race result
• Show integrity by recording and using data accurately in calculations, as modelled by Kenyan athletes and engineers
slo.keyInquiry: What is speed, and how do we calculate velocity and acceleration mathematically?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 2 equips learners with the quantitative tools (v = s/t and a = Δv/Δt) needed to analyse the split-time data from the Nairobi Marathon phenomenon; learners can now calculate exactly how fast each runner was moving during each 5 km segment and how dramatically Runner B's velocity changed — building the mathematical foundation for graphing motion in Lessons 3 and 4.
slo.safetyNotes: No specific hazards. If learners conduct a brief timed walk/jog in the classroom aisle or corridor as part of the Observe phase, ensure the path is clear of bags and furniture to prevent tripping.

LESSONS.overview:
This lesson is the first dedicated calculation lesson in the Linear Motion sequence. Having established in Lesson 1 that distance, displacement, speed, velocity, and acceleration are conceptually distinct, learners now practise computing velocity and acceleration from real data. The anchoring phenomenon — the split-time tables of Runner A and Runner B in the 2023 Nairobi Marathon — provides the raw numbers. Learners calculate the average velocity for each 5 km segment for both runners and immediately see a story emerge: Runner A's velocity is nearly constant (~19 km/h throughout), while Runner B's velocity surges above 21 km/h in the first 10 km, dips to around 16 km/h between 20 km and 30 km, then spikes again to ~22 km/h in the final 12 km. The acceleration values between segments explain why Runner B was ahead at 30 km but lost — the late sprint was too short to overcome the time lost in the slow middle section. Additional worked examples — Eliud Kipchoge's world-record marathon pace, a boda-boda accelerating from rest on Mombasa Road, and the SGR Madaraka Express changing speed between Nairobi and Athi River — anchor the formulas in familiar Kenyan contexts.

The lesson follows the five-phase ARES framework. In the Predict phase, learners estimate Runner B's velocity during the slow middle section before calculating, activating prior knowledge of average speed from Lesson 1. In the Observe phase, learners work in pairs to apply v = s/t to each 5 km split for both runners, generating a velocity table. In the Explain phase, the teacher introduces acceleration formally as a = Δv/Δt and learners calculate the acceleration between selected segments. The DQB phase captures the new insight that a single average speed hides the internal structure of motion, and that acceleration — not just velocity — determines who wins. The Model Building phase has learners annotate their personal motion model (begun in Lesson 1) with calculated values, distinguishing uniform from non-uniform sections.

Throughout, the teacher uses targeted cold-calling, mini-whiteboards (or exercise books held up), and pair-share routines to check procedural accuracy and conceptual understanding simultaneously. The lesson closes with learners writing one sentence on their DQB sticky note answering: "What does speed actually mean mathematically?" — directly advancing the driving question.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners are shown the split-time table from Lesson 1 (projected or on a printed handout) and asked to estimate — without calculating — which 5 km segment they think Runner B ran slowest, and what velocity they guess (in km/h) for that segment. Each learner writes their estimate in their exercise book and shares briefly with their shoulder partner. The class hears three or four estimates read aloud before any calculation begins.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the split-time table and say: 'Before we touch a calculator or do any arithmetic, look at Runner B's times between 20 km and 30 km. In your book, write: (a) which segment you think is the slowest, and (b) your best guess for the velocity in km/h for that segment. You have 60 seconds — work alone first.' [WAIT 60 seconds, circulate, glance at books.] After 60 seconds: 'Turn to your neighbour and compare your guesses. Do you agree? 30 seconds.' [WAIT 30 seconds.] Cold-call 3 learners — choose one high estimate, one low estimate, and one middle estimate — and write the three guesses on the board as a range. Say: 'By the end of today's lesson, we will know the exact answer. Keep your guess written down — we will come back to it.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Anchored Prediction (Estimate-Before-Calculate): Learners commit a numerical estimate to paper before instruction, creating cognitive dissonance if their calculation later differs. This makes the Observe phase calculation feel purposeful — learners are testing their own prediction — and builds number-sense for reasonable velocity magnitudes.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher scans exercise books during the 60-second individual think time, noting whether learners are attempting a rough division (distance ÷ time) or guessing arbitrarily. If most learners write answers between 10 and 30 km/h without any working, this confirms they have some intuitive feel for marathon speeds from Lesson 1. If estimates are wildly outside this range (e.g., 200 km/h or 2 km/h), the teacher notes these learners for targeted support during the Observe phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Working in pairs, learners receive (or refer to) the printed split-time table for Runner A and Runner B. Using the formula v = s/t (velocity = displacement ÷ time for each 5 km segment), each pair completes a structured velocity table for all segments of both runners. They record each velocity in km/h, rounded to one decimal place. Pairs then circle the three fastest and three slowest segments for Runner B and compare their completed velocity table with the prediction made in the Predict phase.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute or direct learners to the split-time data handout. Say: 'We are going to use the formula v = s/t to find the velocity for every 5 km segment. Remember — for each segment, the displacement s is 5 km and the time t is the time Runner A or Runner B took to cover that specific 5 km, not the total race time. Write the formula at the top of your table before you begin.' [WAIT 15 seconds for learners to write the formula.] 'Work with your partner — one person calculates Runner A, the other calculates Runner B, then compare your tables. You have 8 minutes.' [WAIT 8 minutes, circulate actively.] After 4 minutes, pause and do a mid-task check: cold-call 1 pair and ask: 'What velocity did you get for Runner B between 5 km and 10 km?' If the answer is incorrect, ask: 'What did you use as your time for that segment — was it the cumulative time or the split time for just that 5 km?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] Redirect as needed. At 8 minutes: 'Now compare your velocity tables with the guess you made at the start. How close were you? Put a tick if your guess was within 2 km/h, a cross if it was further away.' Cold-call 2 pairs to share their comparison. Then say: 'Look at the velocity column for Runner A. What pattern do you notice?' [WAIT 15 seconds.] Cold-call 3 learners. Expected responses: 'The velocities are nearly the same each segment' / 'Runner A is consistent.' Write on the board: UNIFORM MOTION — velocity stays (approximately) constant. Then: 'Now look at Runner B. What do you see?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] Cold-call 3 different learners. Expected: 'The velocity goes up and down a lot.' Write: NON-UNIFORM MOTION — velocity changes.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data Table Analysis with Phenomenon Connection: Learners generate their own velocity table from raw split-time data rather than receiving pre-calculated values. This mirrors the practice of NGSS Science and Engineering Practice 4 (Analysing and Interpreting Data). Comparing the velocity table back to the prediction activates metacognition. Labelling segments as uniform or non-uniform bridges the calculation to the conceptual vocabulary from Lesson 1.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher checks three specific indicators during circulation: (1) Are learners dividing by the segment time (correct) or the cumulative time (common error)? (2) Are units correct — km/h rather than km/min? (3) Does the completed velocity table show Runner B with a dip between 20–30 km and a spike in the final 12 km? A correct velocity table for Runner B should show approximately: Seg 1–5 km: ~21 km/h, Seg 5–10 km: ~21.5 km/h, Seg 10–15 km: ~20 km/h, Seg 15–20 km: ~18 km/h, Seg 20–25 km: ~16 km/h, Seg 25–30 km: ~16.5 km/h, Seg 30–36 km: ~19 km/h, Seg 36–42 km: ~22 km/h. Any pair whose table diverges significantly is flagged for Explain-phase support.

framework.learnerExperience: The teacher formally introduces acceleration using a = Δv/Δt, connecting it to the velocity changes learners just observed in Runner B's table. Learners follow two teacher-led worked examples (Kipchoge's marathon pace and a boda-boda on Mombasa Road), then independently solve two practice problems — one finding acceleration for Runner B between the slow and sprint sections, and one involving the SGR Madaraka Express. Learners record worked examples and practice solutions in their exercise books.
framework.teacherMoves:
Begin by pointing to the velocity table on the board and say: 'Runner B's velocity changed dramatically between segments. We have a name and a formula for how quickly velocity changes — it is called ACCELERATION.' Write on board: a = Δv ÷ Δt, where Δv = change in velocity (v_final − v_initial) and Δt = time taken for that change. Say: 'The unit of acceleration is metres per second squared, m/s², or kilometres per hour per second, km/h/s, depending on the units we use. Let us do a worked example.' 

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — Kipchoge's Finish Sprint: 'Eliud Kipchoge, the greatest marathon runner in history, increased his velocity from 20.0 km/h to 22.5 km/h in the final 600 m of a race, taking approximately 96 seconds. What was his acceleration?' Write on board step by step: Δv = 22.5 − 20.0 = 2.5 km/h. Convert: 2.5 km/h = 2500 m / 3600 s ≈ 0.694 m/s. Δt = 96 s. a = 0.694 ÷ 96 ≈ 0.0072 m/s². Say: 'That seems small — but for a runner after 42 km, any acceleration is extraordinary. This is why Kipchoge is remarkable.' [Pause 10 seconds — allow learners to finish copying.]

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — Boda-boda on Mombasa Road: 'A boda-boda accelerates from rest at a stage near the Nyayo Stadium roundabout, reaching a velocity of 36 km/h in 10 seconds. Calculate its acceleration in m/s².' Write: v_initial = 0 m/s (rest). v_final = 36 km/h = 36000/3600 = 10 m/s. Δt = 10 s. a = (10 − 0) ÷ 10 = 1 m/s². Say: 'That is a much larger acceleration — the boda-boda changes velocity much faster than Kipchoge did.' Cold-call 1 learner: 'Tell me in words what acceleration of 1 m/s² means.' [WAIT 15 seconds.] Expected: 'Every second, the velocity increases by 1 m/s.' Affirm and write this on the board as a sentence definition.

PRACTICE PROBLEMS — say: 'Now you will try two problems on your own. Write the formula, substitute the values, show all working, state the unit.' [WAIT 10 seconds for learners to prepare.] Problem 1: 'Using Runner B's velocity table, calculate the acceleration between the 20–25 km segment (v ≈ 16 km/h) and the 36–42 km segment (v ≈ 22 km/h). The time for this change was approximately 48 minutes. Is this positive or negative acceleration? What does it mean physically?' Problem 2: 'The SGR Madaraka Express leaves Nairobi Station at rest and reaches a cruising velocity of 120 km/h in 4 minutes. Calculate the acceleration in km/h/min and describe the motion.' [WAIT 6 minutes for individual work. Circulate — note errors in Δv sign convention and unit conversion.] After 6 minutes, cold-call 2 learners to present their solutions on the board. Peer-correct using the protocol: 'Formula correct? Substitution correct? Unit stated? Physical interpretation given?' Close the Explain phase by saying: 'We now have two mathematical tools: v = s/t and a = Δv/Δt. Together, these tell the complete mathematical story of any moving object — including why Runner B lost despite being ahead at 30 km.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Worked Example → Guided Practice → Independent Practice (I Do – We Do – You Do): The teacher models with full narration (Kipchoge, boda-boda), then learners apply independently to phenomenon data (Runner B) and a new Kenyan context (SGR). This gradual release embeds the formulas in multiple real contexts before learners are assessed, strengthening transfer. NGSS Practice 5 (Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking) is explicitly enacted.
framework.formativeAssessment: During independent practice, teacher collects three observable indicators: (1) Correct formula written before substitution — if absent, learner has not internalised the structure. (2) Unit conversion attempted for km/h to m/s or km/h/min — a common sticking point; note learners who skip this step. (3) Physical interpretation written in words — learners who can only produce a number but not interpret it (e.g., 'the velocity increased') have surface-level procedural skill without conceptual understanding. Teacher targets these learners during the DQB phase with a probing question.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner writes one sticky note (or a folded piece of paper if sticky notes are unavailable) answering the prompt: 'What does speed actually mean mathematically, and what NEW question does today's calculation raise for you about the marathon runners?' Learners post their notes on the class DQB under one of three column headers: WHAT WE NOW KNOW | WHAT WE ARE STILL WONDERING | WHAT WE NEED TO FIND OUT. The class briefly reads several contributions aloud.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at our Driving Question: How can we use mathematics — calculations and graphs — to fully describe and explain the motion of any moving body? Today we have added two powerful tools: v = s/t and a = Δv/Δt. On your sticky note, write your answer to this prompt —' [Write on board]: 'Speed means mathematically… AND I am now wondering…' [WAIT 2 minutes for writing.] Collect/post notes. Read aloud 4–5 notes — deliberately choose: one that correctly defines velocity, one that expresses wonder about graphs ('but how do we show this visually?'), one that raises a question about negative acceleration ('what if velocity decreases — is acceleration negative?'), and one that connects to the phenomenon ('I want to know at exactly what point Runner B started slowing down'). After reading, say: 'These questions on the right column — about graphs and about exact turning points — are exactly what Lessons 3 and 4 will answer. Leave them on the board. They are our roadmap.' Circle or highlight DQB notes that mention graphs, turning points, or the word 'deceleration' — these will anchor Lesson 3's launch.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board — Progressive Claim Building: The DQB functions as a public, cumulative record of the class's growing understanding. Posting under three headers (Know / Wondering / Need to Find Out) externalises metacognition and makes the sequence of the unit visible to learners. Teacher curation of selected notes models scientific discourse — not all ideas are equally specific or useful, and the teacher explicitly names why certain questions are productive for the investigation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher reads all DQB notes after class. Key indicators: (a) Does the learner's 'KNOW' statement correctly use the word velocity (vector) rather than just speed (scalar)? (b) Does the 'WONDERING' question point forward to graphs, instantaneous velocity, or deceleration — showing they are thinking beyond today? (c) Are any notes blank or trivially vague ('I wonder about speed')? These learners need a brief check-in at the start of Lesson 3. The teacher photographs the DQB for the ARES platform record.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the personal motion model they began in Lesson 1 — a labelled diagram or annotated timeline of the Nairobi Marathon phenomenon. They now add a second layer to the model: above or beside the timeline, they write the calculated velocity for each 5 km segment of Runner B, and annotate at least two points with the acceleration value and a label (e.g., 'DECELERATING here — a is negative' or 'ACCELERATING here — a is positive'). Learners also add a key to their model distinguishing UNIFORM MOTION sections (Runner A, and Runner B's first 10 km) from NON-UNIFORM MOTION sections (Runner B, 15–30 km and 36–42 km).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your Lesson 1 model — your timeline or diagram of the marathon. You built it with words and arrows. Today we are going to upgrade it with numbers.' Display a partially completed model on the board (teacher-drawn, deliberately incomplete — missing acceleration annotations). Say: 'I have added the velocity numbers above the timeline. What is missing from my model that would help someone understand Runner B's story better?' [WAIT 15 seconds.] Cold-call 2 learners. Expected: 'The acceleration values' / 'Labels for where the runner is speeding up or slowing down.' Say: 'Exactly. Add those two things to your own model now. Also add a key — a small box in the corner that says UNIFORM MOTION (constant velocity) and NON-UNIFORM MOTION (changing velocity), and shows which sections of the race each runner was in. You have 5 minutes.' [WAIT 5 minutes. Circulate and stamp/initial completed models as evidence of engagement.] With 1 minute remaining, say: 'Share your updated model with your partner. Check: does their model show at least one negative acceleration (deceleration) and one positive acceleration? If not, help them add it.' Close by saying: 'Your model is now a mathematical document — it does not just show what happened, it shows how fast and how quickly the velocity changed. Every time we learn something new in this unit, we will come back and add another layer.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision (Progressive Annotation): Learners do not build a new model each lesson — they return to and deepen the same model, adding new conceptual and quantitative layers. This mirrors how scientists revise explanatory models as evidence accumulates (NGSS Practice 2: Developing and Using Models). The teacher's deliberately incomplete board model prompts learners to identify what is missing, rather than simply copying — a higher-order demand.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher looks for three features in each updated model: (1) At least 6 velocity values correctly placed on the Runner B timeline — confirms calculation accuracy from the Observe phase. (2) At least one correctly labelled positive acceleration and one negative acceleration interval — confirms understanding that acceleration has direction/sign. (3) A key or legend that distinguishes uniform from non-uniform motion — confirms conceptual integration. Models missing any of these three features are flagged for the teacher's lesson-start review in Lesson 3.

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
1. During the Observe phase, how many pairs were dividing by the cumulative race time rather than the segment time? What misconception about 'average' does this reveal, and how will I address it explicitly at the start of Lesson 3 before introducing displacement-time graphs?
2. When learners calculated acceleration for Runner B between the slow section and the sprint finish, did they correctly treat the change in velocity as positive (speeding up)? How many learners wrote a negative value, and what does this tell me about their understanding of direction and sign convention in vector quantities?
3. Were the Kenyan contexts (Kipchoge, boda-boda, SGR) genuinely motivating for learners, or did some learners struggle to connect them to the marathon phenomenon? Should I add a third worked example that stays entirely within the marathon data to strengthen the phenomenon thread?
4. Looking at the DQB sticky notes: how many learners spontaneously used the word 'graph' or 'plot' in their WONDERING column? This will tell me how much scaffolding is needed to motivate Lesson 3's displacement-time graph construction.
5. Were learners able to give a verbal/physical interpretation of their acceleration values (e.g., 'the runner's velocity increased by 0.7 km/h every minute'), or did they produce only numerical answers? How will I build the habit of physical interpretation into Lessons 3 and 4 so that graph gradients are understood as rates, not just slopes?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners generated a velocity table for Runner A and Runner B by applying v = s/t to each 5 km split of the 2023 Nairobi Marathon data. They observed that Runner A maintained a nearly constant velocity (~19 km/h) throughout — uniform motion — while Runner B's velocity varied from ~16 km/h in the 20–30 km section to ~22 km/h in the final sprint — non-uniform motion. They also calculated the acceleration of a boda-boda on Mombasa Road (1 m/s²) and the SGR Madaraka Express, and used a = Δv/Δt to find Runner B's acceleration between the slow and fast sections of the race.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Velocity is calculated as v = s/t (displacement divided by time) and is measured in m/s or km/h. Acceleration is calculated as a = Δv/Δt (change in velocity divided by time taken) and is measured in m/s². Uniform motion means constant velocity and zero acceleration; non-uniform motion means changing velocity and non-zero acceleration. A positive acceleration means the object is speeding up; a negative acceleration (deceleration) means it is slowing down. Runner A's near-constant velocity explains his consistent split times; Runner B's large positive and negative accelerations explain why his split times varied so dramatically.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The split-time data from the Nairobi Marathon phenomenon can now be expressed as a sequence of velocities and accelerations — not just a single average speed. Runner B was ahead at 30 km because his early high velocity (positive acceleration off the start) built a time advantage. However, his large negative acceleration (deceleration) between 15 km and 30 km cost him more time than his final sprint could recover. Runner A's near-zero acceleration — uniform motion — meant every segment was equally efficient, and this consistency ultimately won the race. The mathematical tools v = s/t and a = Δv/Δt reveal the internal structure of motion that a single total-time comparison completely hides.

LESSONS.title: Drawing Displacement-Time Graphs: Reading the Shape of the Race

slo.purpose: Learners plot and interpret displacement-time graphs using the Nairobi Marathon split-time data and their own school-race data, connecting graph shape to the physical motion of the runners.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, learners will know: (a) the conventions for drawing a displacement-time graph (labelled axes, correct units, appropriate scale, title); (b) that a straight line on a displacement-time graph represents constant speed; (c) that a horizontal line represents rest (zero velocity); (d) that a steeper line represents higher speed; and (e) that a downward slope represents motion back towards the starting point.
slo.skills: By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to: (a) plot a displacement-time graph accurately on squared paper from a given data table; (b) predict the general shape of a displacement-time graph before plotting; (c) interpret sections of a displacement-time graph to describe the motion at each stage; and (d) compare two displacement-time graphs plotted on the same axes to explain the outcome of the Nairobi Marathon race.
slo.attitudes: Learners will: (a) appreciate that a graph communicates the full story of motion far more richly than a single number; (b) demonstrate integrity by plotting points accurately and not 'tidying up' a curved section into a straight line; and (c) demonstrate unity by collaborating in pairs during the plotting activity and respecting each other's observations.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we use displacement-time graphs in real life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 1 learners measured and compared distance, displacement, speed, and velocity using their own school-race data. In Lesson 2 they calculated average speed and velocity for Runner A and Runner B from the marathon split-time table. In this lesson (Lesson 3) they move from numerical calculations to graphical representation: they plot both runners' split-time data on the same displacement-time graph, predict the shape before plotting, and use the graph's shape — not just its endpoints — to explain why Runner A won despite Runner B leading at 30 km. This is the first time learners see that the gradient of a line segment equals speed, preparing Lesson 4's formal treatment of gradient and Lesson 5's velocity-time graphs.
slo.safetyNotes: No hazardous materials. Ensure learners use rulers with clean edges to avoid inaccurate plotting. Remind learners not to press so hard with pencils that they tear squared paper. If compasses are used to mark arcs, remind learners to handle pointed ends carefully.

LESSONS.overview: Learners open with a sketch-prediction task: without any calculation, they sketch what they think Runner A's and Runner B's displacement-time graphs will look like, annotating with reasons. They then gather evidence by plotting both runners' split-time tables (from the Nairobi Marathon data printout introduced in Lesson 1) on the same pair of axes on squared paper, following taught conventions. A structured class discussion unpacks what different line shapes (steep, gentle, horizontal, downward) mean physically. Learners return to their predictions, annotate discrepancies, and use the completed graph to write a 'race commentary' explaining exactly when and why Runner B lost the lead. The lesson closes with a Driving Question Board update and a one-sentence exit ticket linking graph gradient to speed.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner receives a blank displacement-time axis template (displacement in km on the y-axis, time in minutes on the x-axis, both unlabelled deliberately). Working individually for 5 minutes, learners sketch — without plotting exact points — what they expect Runner A's and Runner B's lines to look like, based only on what they already know: Runner A runs at a nearly constant pace; Runner B starts fast, slows in the middle, and sprints at the end. Learners annotate each sketch with at least two reasons justifying the shape they drew. They fold and keep their prediction sketches to compare after plotting.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the blank axis templates. Say: 'Before we touch the data table, I want you to be a mathematician — make a prediction. You already know from Lesson 2 how fast each runner was at different stages. Now show me what that LOOKS like as a picture. Work alone for 5 minutes.' Circulate and observe without correcting. After 5 minutes, cold-call 3 learners: 'Achieng, hold up your sketch and tell us ONE thing you drew for Runner B.' Apply 10 seconds wait time before calling. Repeat for 2 more learners. Do NOT reveal answers. Say: 'We are going to find out if your predictions are right. Keep your sketches — you will need them at the end of the lesson.' Write on the board: PREDICTION SEALED. Do not discuss correctness yet.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-first sketching (pre-assessment elicitation). By committing a sketch to paper before instruction, learners activate and expose their existing mental models of motion. This creates cognitive dissonance when the plotted graph differs from their expectation, which is the engine of sensemaking. The teacher's deliberate silence about correctness sustains productive uncertainty.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: every learner has produced a sketch with at least one labelled annotation before Phase 2 begins. Teacher scans for two common misconceptions to address later: (1) learners who draw Runner B's line as always above Runner A's (confusing 'ahead in distance' with 'faster'); (2) learners who draw a curve where they should draw connected straight line segments. Note names of learners holding each misconception for targeted cold-calling in Phase 3.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in pairs. Each pair receives: (a) the Nairobi Marathon split-time data printout (first seen in Lesson 1) showing Runner A and Runner B's cumulative displacement (km) at every 5 km checkpoint and the corresponding elapsed time (minutes); (b) a sheet of A4 squared paper; (c) a ruler and two coloured pencils (e.g. blue for Runner A, red for Runner B). Step 1 (8 min): The teacher models — on the board using a large grid — how to set up the axes: x-axis = Time (minutes), scale 0–260 min, 1 cm = 20 min; y-axis = Displacement from start (km), scale 0–42 km, 1 cm = 5 km. Learners copy axes, add a title ('Displacement-Time Graph: 2023 Nairobi Marathon — Runner A vs Runner B'), and label axes with units. Step 2 (12 min): Pairs plot all data points for Runner A (blue) and connect with straight line segments between consecutive checkpoints. Step 3 (8 min): Pairs plot Runner B's points (red) on the SAME axes and connect. Step 4 (2 min): Learners circle in pencil the point on the graph where Runner B's line crosses Runner A's line for the second time (the overtake and then the re-overtake). This is the graphical answer to the driving question phenomenon.
framework.teacherMoves: At the board, demonstrate axis setup explicitly: 'Watch — I am choosing my scale so ALL my data fits AND I can read the graph clearly. Time goes on the horizontal axis — always. Displacement goes on the vertical axis — always. My title tells the reader exactly what this graph shows.' Plot the first two points for Runner A on the board while narrating each step. Then say: 'Now YOUR turn — plot all of Runner A's points first, connect them, then do Runner B. You have 20 minutes.' Circulate every 90 seconds. At 8 minutes, pause the class: 'Hold up your paper — I want to see Runner A's line. Good. Now continue with Runner B.' If a pair has a wildly incorrect scale, crouch beside them and ask: 'Your highest y-value is 42 km — how many squares do you have? What scale will let everything fit?' (Do NOT draw it for them.) At 18 minutes, cold-call 2 pairs to describe in one sentence what they notice about where the two lines cross. Apply 12 seconds wait time. Say: 'Circle that crossing point — that is the moment we need to explain.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Dual-representation plotting (concrete-to-graphical bridging). Learners simultaneously hold the numerical data table and the emerging graph, building the connection between a row of numbers and a point on a plane. Using two colours for the two runners on the same axes allows direct visual comparison — a strategy that makes the 'Runner B was ahead at 30 km' phenomenon visible as a spatial relationship rather than an abstract claim.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Both lines are plotted with correct units and a title — teacher checks during circulation. (2) The crossing point is correctly identified at approximately t = 220 min, d = 38 km. (3) Line segments are straight between checkpoints (not smoothed into a curve) — if learners draw a curve, ask: 'Do we KNOW what happened between the 30 km and 35 km checkpoints? We only have data at those two points — so we connect them with a straight line.' Record pairs who struggle with scale choice for targeted support in Phase 3.

framework.learnerExperience: Whole-class discussion and individual written analysis. Learners use their completed dual graph to answer five structured questions written on the board (or printed on an analysis strip): Q1 — Which section of Runner A's graph is steepest? What does that tell you about their speed at that point? Q2 — Find a section of Runner B's graph that is less steep than the section before it. What was Runner B doing? Q3 — If Runner B had completely stopped at a water station, what would their graph look like at that point? Q4 — Using your graph, estimate the time (in minutes) at which Runner B was furthest ahead of Runner A. Q5 — Write a 'race commentary' of three sentences describing Runner B's race using only the language of graph shape (steep, gentle, horizontal). Learners write answers individually (8 min), then share with their pair (3 min). Teacher leads a whole-class debrief (9 min). Learners then retrieve their original prediction sketches, compare with actual graph, and annotate in a third colour: 'I predicted correctly that… / I was surprised that…'
framework.teacherMoves: Post the five questions. Say: 'These questions can ALL be answered by looking at your graph — you do not need to calculate anything yet. Read the graph like you read a story.' Give 8 minutes individual work. Circulate and identify at least one learner who has correctly linked steepness to speed (to affirm publicly) and one who has answered Q3 by drawing a horizontal line in the air (to cold-call). After 8 minutes: 'Share your Q1 answer with your partner. 30 seconds.' Then cold-call: 'Kipchoge — for Q1, which section did you find steepest for Runner A? Tell us why that means high speed.' [Wait 12 seconds.] Affirm: 'Exactly — steeper slope, same time interval, MORE displacement covered. That IS speed.' For Q3, ask: 'Wanjiru, if Runner B stopped completely, what does the graph look like at that moment?' [Wait 10 seconds.] Draw a small horizontal segment on the board: 'A horizontal line means displacement is NOT changing — the runner is stationary.' Then: 'Get out your original prediction sketches. Annotate them right now — two differences you see between your prediction and your actual graph.' Cold-call one learner to share a surprise. Connect to phenomenon: 'So now look at your graph — where EXACTLY did Runner B lose the race? Point to it.' [Learners point.] 'That single moment is what our graph can show that Runner B's average speed — 4.27 m/s — could NEVER show us.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Graph-as-narrative strategy (slope = story). Learners are explicitly taught to 'read' a graph as a sequence of events rather than as a shape to be memorised. By writing a three-sentence race commentary using graph-shape vocabulary, they verbalise the connection between gradient magnitude and speed — the key conceptual bridge to Lesson 4's formal gradient calculation. The prediction-comparison annotation makes metacognitive revision visible and valued.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Q1 answer correctly identifies the steepest segment and uses the word 'speed' or 'fast' — teacher listens during cold-calling. (2) Q3 answer describes or draws a horizontal line — teacher checks written work. (3) Race commentary (Q5) contains at least one correct graph-shape descriptor linked to a physical event (e.g., 'Runner B's line becomes less steep between 25 km and 35 km, showing they were slowing down'). (4) Prediction annotations exist in a third colour on every learner's original sketch — teacher scans during circulation.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board. Working in their pairs, they write on a sticky note or card (colour-coded: green = new understanding, orange = new question): one thing they can NOW explain about the marathon phenomenon that they could not explain before this lesson, and one new question the graph has raised for them. Pairs post their cards on the DQB in the appropriate columns: 'What we can now explain' and 'What we still need to find out.' The teacher reads three cards aloud to the class and briefly annotates the DQB, highlighting the cluster of questions around 'How do we find the exact speed from the graph?' as the bridge to Lesson 4.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'We now have a graph that tells the full story of the race. Update our Driving Question Board. Write: one thing you can now EXPLAIN — use the word graph in your answer. And one thing your graph has made you MORE curious about.' Give 4 minutes for writing and posting. Read three posted cards aloud — choose one strong 'explain' card, one weak/vague card (to model improving it), and one 'new question' card that foreshadows gradient. Say: 'Several of you asked HOW we calculate the exact speed from a graph — not just say it is steep, but get a number. That is exactly what we investigate in Lesson 4. Your graph is not finished — it is a TOOL we will keep using.' Point to the DQB column 'What we still need to find out' and say: 'These questions are our roadmap for the next five lessons.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board update (knowledge-tracking protocol). By requiring learners to articulate both new understanding and new questions, the DQB update externalises the cumulative nature of the evidence-gathering sequence. The colour-coding (green/orange) allows the teacher and learners to see at a glance how the class's collective understanding is growing lesson by lesson, and sustains the motivating puzzle of the phenomenon across all 8 lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Every pair has posted at least one green and one orange card. (2) 'Explain' cards reference graph shape or the marathon phenomenon specifically — not generic statements like 'I learned about graphs.' (3) New questions are answerable through future lessons (i.e., they are mathematically productive), not purely factual questions about the marathon event.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open the cumulative model they began in Lesson 1 (a written/drawn model of 'how motion works' that they revise each lesson). Today's revision task: add the displacement-time graph of Runner A and Runner B to the model, with a key that links each type of line segment (steep, gentle, horizontal) to the physical meaning. Learners add one sentence in their own words: 'The gradient of a displacement-time graph tells us…' — they complete this sentence based on what they have reasoned today (they are not yet given the formal gradient formula; they write it in descriptive language, e.g., 'how quickly displacement is changing, which is the speed'). Learners share their completed sentence with a shoulder partner, then one sentence is chosen by the teacher to be written on a class anchor chart that will be added to each lesson.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your cumulative model from Lesson 1. Today you are adding the graphical layer. Stick or draw a small version of your displacement-time graph into your model. Then add a KEY — three entries: steep line = ?, gentle line = ?, horizontal line = ?. Fill in the physical meaning for each.' Give 5 minutes. Then: 'Now complete this sentence at the bottom of your model page: The gradient of a displacement-time graph tells us… — do not use the word gradient in your answer; explain it in plain language.' Give 2 minutes. Cold-call 2 learners to read their sentence. [10 seconds wait time each.] Choose the clearest sentence and write it on the anchor chart under 'Lesson 3 — Displacement-Time Graph.' Say: 'In Lesson 4 we will make this sentence more precise by calculating the gradient as a number. You have already discovered the idea — next lesson you will make it mathematical.' Collect squared-paper graphs for teacher review (return in Lesson 4).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision (progressive model building). The model acts as a personalised 'theory of motion' that grows across all 8 lessons. Adding the graph and the gradient sentence today makes the conceptual progression explicit: learners can literally see, by flipping back through their model, how their understanding has deepened from 'motion is distance and time' (Lesson 1) to 'motion is the shape of a graph' (Lesson 3) to, eventually, 'motion is the calculus of area and gradient' (Lessons 6–8). The unfinished sentence about gradient creates a productive anticipation for Lesson 4.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) The model key correctly pairs steep/gentle/horizontal with faster/slower/stationary. (2) The gradient sentence, in the learner's own words, correctly captures the idea of rate of change of displacement (even if not using that terminology). (3) Learners who write 'the gradient tells us the distance' (confusing displacement with speed) are identified and their papers are flagged for targeted re-teaching at the start of Lesson 4. Teacher collects all graphs to check: correct scales, labelled axes, title, two colours, and crossing point circled.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: (1) PREDICTION QUALITY — Did the majority of learners predict that Runner B's line would be steeper initially and then flatten? If most drew two similar straight lines, it suggests Lesson 2's speed calculations were not yet connected to the idea of varying speed — revisit by opening Lesson 4 with a 5-minute recap of Runner B's checkpoint-by-checkpoint speeds. (2) SCALE CHOICE — How many pairs needed direct teacher intervention to choose a workable scale? If more than a third of pairs struggled, build a dedicated 5-minute 'scale-choice protocol' into the start of Lesson 4 before gradient work begins. (3) GRAPH-AS-NARRATIVE — Were learners able to write a race commentary (Q5) that used graph-shape language? If answers defaulted to 'Runner B was fast then slow,' without referencing line shape, the gradient-language bridge to Lesson 4 is not yet secure — use those written responses as worked examples at the start of Lesson 4. (4) DQB QUALITY — Did new questions cluster around 'how do we get a number from the steepness?' If so, this is the ideal launch point for Lesson 4. If questions were mostly about the marathon event itself (e.g., 'Who was Runner B?'), redirect the DQB in Lesson 4 by asking: 'Which of these questions can mathematics answer — and how?'

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners plotted the split-time data for Runner A and Runner B from the 2023 Nairobi Marathon on the same displacement-time graph using squared paper, two colours, labelled axes, and a title. They circled the point where Runner B's line crossed Runner A's line for the final time — the graphical moment that explains the race outcome.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The shape of a displacement-time graph — not just its start and end points — tells the full story of motion. A steep line means high speed; a gentle line means low speed; a horizontal line means the runner is stationary. The gradient of the line at any section represents the speed of the runner at that stage of the race.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Using the completed dual displacement-time graph, learners explained why Runner B — despite being ahead at 30 km — lost the race: Runner B's line became noticeably less steep between 25 km and 38 km (slowing down), while Runner A's line maintained a consistent gradient throughout, overtaking Runner B with approximately 4 km remaining. A single average-speed calculation could never have revealed this — only the graph shape can.

LESSONS.title: Interpreting Displacement-Time Graphs: Gradient as Velocity

slo.purpose: Learners interpret pre-drawn displacement-time graphs representing real-life Kenyan scenarios, calculate the gradient of each segment, and connect gradient to velocity — enabling them to read the full story of motion from a graph's shape.
slo.knowledge: Learners will know that: (a) the gradient of a displacement-time graph equals velocity; (b) a steeper positive gradient means higher velocity; (c) a zero gradient (horizontal segment) means the object is stationary; (d) a negative gradient means the object is returning towards its starting point; (e) average velocity over an interval is calculated as change in displacement ÷ change in time.
slo.skills: Learners will be able to: (a) read displacement and time values from a multi-segment graph; (b) calculate the gradient of each segment and state its meaning in context; (c) identify stationary, constant-velocity, and return phases from graph shape; (d) construct a brief narrative of motion from a displacement-time graph; (e) use gradient calculations to compare velocities of two moving bodies.
slo.attitudes: Learners will: (a) appreciate that a graph communicates richer information than a single number; (b) show integrity by reading graph values carefully and recording calculations honestly; (c) show responsibility by connecting mathematical results back to real-world meaning.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we use displacement-time graphs in real life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 3, learners drew displacement-time graphs from the Marathon split-time data and noticed that the shapes for Runner A and Runner B were different. In this lesson they move from drawing to systematic interpretation — calculating gradients segment by segment to quantify what each part of the graph reveals about velocity. By the end of the lesson, learners can fully answer Key Inquiry Question 2 and can update their Driving Question Board entry explaining exactly why Runner B was ahead at 30 km yet lost: his gradient (velocity) in the final segment was lower than Runner A's sprint gradient.
slo.safetyNotes: No physical hazards. Learners use rulers and pencils on printed graph sheets — remind learners to handle rulers carefully and not to lean on sharp edges. Ensure printed graph sheets are distributed before the lesson to avoid delays.

LESSONS.overview: Lesson 4 of 8 in the evidence-gathering sequence for Sub-Strand 2.9: Linear Motion. Learners receive a set of four pre-drawn displacement-time graphs on a printed worksheet. Each graph depicts a different Kenyan scenario: (1) a matatu travelling from Nakuru town centre, stopping at a stage, then continuing; (2) a marathon runner resting at a water station on Uhuru Highway; (3) a boda-boda rider cycling away from home and then returning; (4) an SGR Madaraka Express multi-stop journey between Nairobi and Mombasa. Using the Predict–Observe–Explain framework, learners first predict what each graph segment means, then systematically calculate gradients, then construct written motion narratives. The lesson culminates in DQB revision — learners update their board to answer "How do we use displacement-time graphs in real life?" — and a cumulative model revision linking gradient-as-velocity back to the Marathon phenomenon. The SGR data anchors the lesson in authentic Kenyan infrastructure and provides rich multi-segment gradient work.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners receive the printed worksheet containing four displacement-time graphs (no labels on the y-axis segments, only axes with scales). Working individually for 4 minutes, then sharing with a partner for 2 minutes, each learner writes answers to three prediction prompts printed at the top of the worksheet: (1) 'Look at Graph 1 — the matatu. Which segment do you think shows the matatu stopped at a stage? How can you tell just from the shape?' (2) 'In Graph 3 — the boda-boda — one segment slopes downward. What do you think that means about the rider's position?' (3) 'Without calculating anything, rank the four segments of Graph 4 (the SGR journey) from fastest to slowest. What visual clue did you use?' Learners write predictions in their exercise books before any instruction is given.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the worksheet face-down. Say: 'Do NOT turn it over until I say so.' After all sheets are distributed, say: 'Turn over. You have 4 minutes — write your predictions for the three questions at the top. I am not looking for right answers; I want your honest thinking right now.' Start a visible timer. Circulate silently — do not answer questions, only prompt with: 'Write something — even if you are not sure.' At 4 minutes, say: 'Now turn to your partner. Share your prediction for Question 2 only. You have 90 seconds.' After partner share, cold-call 3 pairs (choose one high-confidence, one mid-confidence, one uncertain based on circulation observations). For each, ask: 'What did your pair say — and what is your reasoning?' Allow 10 seconds WAIT TIME after each response before acknowledging. Do NOT correct errors yet. Record 2–3 key student predictions visibly on the board under the heading 'Our Predictions — Before Evidence'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Strategy: Prediction Anchoring. By committing predictions to paper before instruction, learners activate prior intuitions about graph shape and motion. This creates a cognitive 'hook' — when the correct interpretation is later established through gradient calculation, the contrast with their prediction deepens understanding. Displaying predictions on the board also creates accountability: learners are motivated to check whether their intuition was right during the Observe phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Every learner has at least one written prediction per prompt before partner share begins. Teacher scans for two specific misconceptions to address later: (a) learners who say a downward slope means 'slowing down' (confusing gradient sign with gradient magnitude — it means returning, not decelerating); (b) learners who rank SGR segments by length of segment rather than steepness. Note names of learners holding these misconceptions for targeted cold-calling in Phase 3.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work through the four graphs systematically in pairs using the structured 'Gradient Hunter' table printed on the reverse of their worksheet. The table has columns: Segment | Start point (t, s) | End point (t, s) | Change in displacement (Δs) | Change in time (Δt) | Gradient = Δs/Δt | Units | What this tells us about velocity. For Graphs 1–3, learners complete all segments (2–3 segments each). For Graph 4 (SGR Nairobi–Mombasa), they complete 5 segments representing: Nairobi departure → Athi River stop; Athi River → Emali stop; Emali → Mtito Andei stop; Mtito Andei → Voi stop; Voi → Mombasa arrival. A horizontal segment (Mtito Andei rest stop, 10 minutes) is deliberately included. Learners read coordinates directly from the graph, substitute into the gradient formula, record units as km/min or km/h (conversion prompt provided), and write a one-sentence motion description for each segment. Time allocation: 18 minutes for pair work.
framework.teacherMoves: Before releasing pairs to work, model the gradient calculation ONCE using a projected or board-drawn mini-graph (not one of the four on the worksheet). Say: 'I am going to show you the method using this example — a matatu travelling from Nairobi CBD to Westlands. Watch what I do.' Draw two points, read coordinates aloud, calculate Δs and Δt, divide, state units, write: "The matatu travelled at 0.8 km/min, which is 48 km/h." Then say: 'Now you do the same for your four graphs. Work in pairs — one person reads the coordinates, the other records and calculates. Swap roles after each graph.' Set a 18-minute timer. Circulate with purpose: (1) At 5 minutes — check that all pairs have correctly identified the horizontal segment on Graph 2 (runner resting) and have written gradient = 0; if not, ask 'What is the change in displacement during this segment?' and wait 10 seconds. (2) At 10 minutes — check Graph 4 Mtito Andei segment: ask 'What does a gradient of zero mean in the context of the SGR train?' (3) At 15 minutes — check units: prompt any pair writing 'km' instead of 'km/min' with: 'Gradient = Δs ÷ Δt — what are the units of each?' After 18 minutes, cold-call 4 pairs (one per graph) to share ONE gradient value and its motion meaning. Allow 10 seconds WAIT TIME per response. Write correct gradient values on board in a summary column.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Strategy: Structured Data Table (Gradient Hunter). The pre-formatted table scaffolds the mathematical procedure into discrete retrievable steps, preventing learners from skipping to an answer without connecting Δs and Δt. Writing a one-sentence motion description for every segment forces translation between symbolic result and physical meaning — a key sensemaking move that connects mathematics to the Marathon phenomenon. The SGR multi-segment graph mirrors the Marathon split-time structure, making the connection explicit.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) All pairs correctly record gradient = 0 with description 'stationary / not moving' for the horizontal SGR segment and the runner's rest segment. (b) At least one member of each pair can state the units of gradient as km/min or km/h without prompting. (c) Pairs correctly identify that the negative-gradient segment on the boda-boda graph means the rider is returning home (displacement decreasing), not slowing down. Teacher notes any pair still writing 'slowing down' for the negative segment — these pairs are prioritised in Phase 3.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to individual work for the 'Motion Narrator' task (12 minutes). Using their completed Gradient Hunter tables, each learner writes a full motion narrative for ONE assigned graph (teacher assigns each pair a graph by calling table numbers). The narrative must: (a) state the starting and ending displacement; (b) name each phase (e.g., 'constant velocity phase', 'stationary phase', 'return phase'); (c) quote the calculated gradient as the velocity in each phase; (d) compare two segments and explain which shows higher velocity and why. After individual writing (8 minutes), pairs join to form groups of four and compare narratives for the same graph — identifying agreements and resolving any differences in interpretation (4 minutes). Each group then nominates one speaker to present their narrative to the class in a 60-second 'pitch'. The class listens and can challenge with: 'Show me which segment you are describing on the graph.'
framework.teacherMoves: Before individual writing begins, address the two key misconceptions identified in Phase 1 directly. Write on the board: 'CLAIM: A downward slope means the object is slowing down.' Ask the class: 'Agree or disagree? Use your gradient calculation from the boda-boda graph as evidence. 10 seconds to think.' Cold-call a learner who was noted holding this misconception. After their response, probe: 'What is the value of the gradient in that segment? What does the negative sign tell us about direction, not speed?' Then write the correct statement: 'A negative gradient means displacement is DECREASING — the object is moving back toward the origin.' During individual writing, circulate and look for: learners who quote gradient correctly as velocity with units; learners who correctly use the phrase 'constant velocity' for straight-line segments. After group comparison and pitches, facilitate a whole-class discussion using the question: 'Runner B in our Marathon was ahead at 30 km. Looking at what we just learned about gradient — what would Runner B's displacement-time graph look like in the final 12 km compared to Runner A's? Which graph shape wins the race?' Allow 15 seconds WAIT TIME. Cold-call 3 learners. Summarise on the board: 'Higher gradient in the final segment = higher velocity = Runner A wins.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Strategy: Motion Narrator (Claim–Evidence–Reasoning writing). Translating a graph into a full written narrative requires learners to hold the mathematical result (gradient value) and its physical meaning (velocity) simultaneously, then sequence them into a coherent story. This is precisely the sensemaking required to answer the driving question. The group comparison step surfaces conflicting interpretations and requires evidence-based resolution — mirroring scientific argumentation practice (NGSS SEP 7: Engaging in Argument from Evidence). Connecting back to Runner A vs Runner B re-anchors the lesson in the phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) Each learner's written narrative contains at least one correctly quoted gradient value with units used as velocity. (b) Narratives correctly distinguish between 'stationary' (gradient = 0), 'constant velocity' (non-zero constant gradient), and 'returning' (negative gradient). (c) During the Marathon connection discussion, at least 3 cold-called learners can articulate that a steeper positive gradient in the final segment explains Runner A's win — linking graph interpretation directly to the phenomenon. Teacher uses a quick show-of-hands: 'Thumbs up if you can now explain, using the word gradient, why Runner A won' — target: ≥ 75% of class.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board displayed at the front. The board has been carrying sticky notes and questions from Lessons 1–3. Key Inquiry Question 2 — 'How do we use displacement-time graphs in real life?' — has been on the board since Lesson 1. Each learner now writes a new sticky note (green = answer, yellow = new question still open) and places it on the board. Their green note must answer KIQ 2 in 1–2 sentences using the word 'gradient'. Their yellow note (optional but encouraged) raises a new question — for example: 'What if the gradient is changing — the line is curved? Does that mean acceleration?' or 'Can we find the velocity at a single moment, not just over a segment?' The teacher then facilitates a 4-minute whole-class DQB review: reading 3–4 selected green notes aloud and 2–3 yellow notes. Yellow notes that anticipate velocity-time graphs or acceleration are explicitly affirmed: 'Excellent — that is exactly what we will need in Lesson 5.'
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute green and yellow sticky notes. Say: 'You now have evidence from four real Kenyan scenarios. On your GREEN note, answer this question — write it exactly as it appears on the board: How do we use displacement-time graphs in real life? Your answer must include the word gradient. On your YELLOW note, write something you are still wondering about — something today's lesson raised but did not answer. You have 3 minutes.' Set timer. Circulate — if any learner's green note omits 'gradient', tap the board and say quietly: 'Check the key word.' After notes are placed, read 3 green notes aloud without naming the author. After each, ask the class: 'Does this answer satisfy the question? Thumbs up or down.' For yellow notes, read 2 aloud and say: 'We are going to need these questions in Lesson 5. Hold onto those thoughts.' Point to the still-unanswered DQB section: 'Look — our big driving question is still not fully answered. We can now explain what happened at every point of the race using gradient. But we still cannot fully explain the sprint — what happens when velocity is changing rapidly. That is our next investigation.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Strategy: Driving Question Board Revision (public knowledge-building). The DQB functions as a communal sensemaking artefact — it externalises the class's growing understanding and makes gaps visible. Moving a question from 'unanswered' to 'answered' by placing a green note is a motivating, metacognitive act. Yellow notes activate productive curiosity about curved graphs and instantaneous velocity, creating a natural bridge to Lessons 5–6 (velocity-time graphs and acceleration). This strategy reflects NGSS SEP 1 (Asking Questions) and SEP 6 (Constructing Explanations).
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) Every learner places at least one green note containing the word 'gradient' and a real-life context reference. (b) At least 40% of learners place a yellow note that references changing velocity, curves, or acceleration — indicating readiness for Lesson 5. (c) During the class vote on green notes, ≥ 80% of thumbs are up, indicating broad class consensus on the answer to KIQ 2. Teacher photographs the updated DQB board for reference in Lesson 5.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to their cumulative 'Motion Story Model' — a personal annotated diagram they have been building since Lesson 1. This model currently shows: a timeline of the Marathon with distance markers; an annotated split-time table distinguishing Runner A and Runner B; and a displacement-time sketch graph drawn in Lesson 3. In this lesson, learners add a new layer to their model: they annotate each segment of their Runner A vs Runner B displacement-time sketch graph with the calculated gradient (velocity) value, using coloured pens. They must label at least: the segment where Runner B leads (steeper gradient, higher velocity in km/min), the water-station segment (horizontal, gradient = 0), and the final sprint segment (comparing gradients of the two runners, showing Runner A's is steeper). Below their annotated graph, learners write one 'Model Claim' statement: 'I can now explain [part of the phenomenon] because I know that [gradient concept].' Learners who finish early are challenged to sketch what a curved displacement-time segment would look like and annotate it with a question.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your Motion Story Model to the displacement-time sketch you added in Lesson 3. Today we are going to make it speak — we are going to annotate every segment with its gradient value and what that means about velocity.' Give 2 minutes for learners to retrieve their models. Display a model example (teacher's own annotated version projected or drawn on board) showing the annotation style: arrow pointing to a segment → gradient value → velocity interpretation in words. Say: 'Your model must show: the segment where Runner B is winning — label its gradient. The water-station stop — label its gradient. The final 12 km sprint — label both Runner A's gradient and Runner B's gradient and circle the winner.' Circulate for 8 minutes. Look for: correct gradient values transferred from the Gradient Hunter table; correct winner identification based on gradient comparison. After 8 minutes, cold-call 2 learners to read their 'Model Claim' statement aloud. After each, ask the class: 'Does this claim use the evidence we gathered today? Thumbs up or down.' Close the lesson by saying: 'Your model can now explain every straight-line phase of this race. But look at your graph — do the lines ever curve? In Lesson 5, we will discover what a curve on this graph means, and that will lead us to velocity-time graphs and acceleration — the final tools we need to explain the sprint finish completely.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Strategy: Cumulative Model Annotation (Progressive Model Revision). Annotating a previously drawn graph with newly calculated gradient values enacts NGSS SEP 2 (Developing and Using Models) — the model becomes more explanatory with each lesson. The 'Model Claim' writing exercise forces each learner to articulate the specific conceptual gain of this lesson in their own words, supporting metacognitive awareness of learning progression. Connecting back to the still-unexplained curved sprint segment creates purposeful incompleteness — a pedagogical strategy that sustains curiosity for Lesson 5.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) Every learner's annotated graph shows at least three labelled gradient values with correct units and correct motion interpretation (stationary, constant velocity, or return). (b) Every learner correctly circles Runner A's final segment as having the higher gradient (velocity) and writes this as the reason Runner A won. (c) 'Model Claim' statements reference gradient and velocity explicitly. (d) Extension learners sketch a curved segment and annotate it with a meaningful question — teacher notes these for use as a launch prompt in Lesson 5. Teacher collects 5–6 models at random for informal marking before Lesson 5.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following questions: (1) Misconception check — Did learners consistently distinguish between a negative gradient (returning toward origin) and a decreasing gradient (decelerating)? If more than 25% of learners' green DQB notes or model annotations conflated these two ideas, plan a 5-minute re-teach at the start of Lesson 5 using the boda-boda graph. (2) Gradient calculation accuracy — Were learners reading coordinates precisely enough from the graph, or did rounding errors lead to significantly different gradient values across pairs? If so, consider adding a 'coordinate reading' mini-drill to Lesson 5's opening. (3) Phenomenon connection — Did learners successfully transfer gradient-as-velocity from the worksheet graphs back to the Marathon phenomenon during the DQB and model phases? If the Marathon connection felt forced rather than natural, review the transition question in Phase 3 and Phase 5. (4) DQB yellow notes — Were learners' yellow notes pointing meaningfully toward acceleration and velocity-time graphs? This is the key readiness indicator for Lesson 5. Count the yellow notes referencing 'changing velocity', 'curve', or 'acceleration' — target is ≥ 40% of class. (5) Pacing — The Observe phase (Gradient Hunter, 18 minutes) is the most time-intensive. If pairs did not complete Graph 4 (SGR), assign the remaining SGR segments as a 5-minute starter activity in Lesson 5 rather than cutting Phase 4 or Phase 5.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners examined four pre-drawn displacement-time graphs showing Kenyan real-life motion scenarios: a matatu stopping at a Nakuru stage, a marathon runner resting at a water station on Uhuru Highway, a boda-boda rider returning home, and the SGR Madaraka Express making stops between Nairobi and Mombasa. Using the Gradient Hunter table, learners read coordinates from each segment and calculated gradient values for every phase of each journey.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Learners established that the gradient of a displacement-time graph equals velocity; a zero gradient means the object is stationary; a negative gradient means the object is returning toward its starting point; and a steeper positive gradient means higher velocity. Learners applied this to the Marathon phenomenon by annotating Runner A and Runner B's sketch graphs with segment gradient values and identifying that Runner A's higher gradient in the final 12 km sprint is the mathematical explanation for why Runner A won despite being behind at 30 km.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Learners explained that displacement-time graphs are used in real life to reveal the velocity at every phase of a journey — not just the overall average. By calculating the gradient of each segment, we can identify when a body was moving fast, slow, stationary, or returning. This answers Key Inquiry Question 2: we use displacement-time graphs to describe and compare motion in detail, segment by segment, which a single average speed calculation cannot do.
