LESSONS.title: Drawing Velocity-Time Graphs — Reading Acceleration in the Shape of the Race
LESSONS.aresKeywords: velocity-time graph, acceleration, gradient, linear motion, uniform velocity

slo.purpose: Learners construct velocity-time graphs from data tables and identify gradient as acceleration, building the mathematical tools needed to fully explain Runner B's dramatic sprint finish at the 2023 Nairobi Marathon.
slo.knowledge:
• A velocity-time graph plots velocity (y-axis, m/s or km/h) against time (x-axis, seconds or minutes)
• The gradient of a velocity-time graph equals acceleration: a = Δv/Δt
• A horizontal segment on a velocity-time graph represents constant velocity (zero acceleration)
• A positive gradient means the object is accelerating (speeding up); a negative gradient means deceleration (slowing down)
• The steeper the gradient, the greater the magnitude of acceleration
slo.skills:
• Draw an accurate velocity-time graph from a given table of values, including correct labelling of axes, units, scale, and title
• Calculate the gradient of each segment of a velocity-time graph and interpret it as acceleration in m/s²
• Identify and describe phases of uniform motion, acceleration, and deceleration from graph shape
slo.attitudes:
• Appreciate that a graph's shape — not just its end points — reveals the full story of motion, reflecting integrity in mathematical representation
• Show responsibility by plotting data carefully and accurately, recognising that precision in mathematics mirrors precision in real-world measurement
slo.keyInquiry: How do we use velocity-time graphs?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 3 and 4 learners mastered displacement-time graphs and gradient as velocity. Lesson 5 advances the storyline by introducing velocity-time graphs, allowing learners to visualise and calculate acceleration directly — the missing mathematical tool needed to explain why Runner B's powerful but unsustained sprint in the final 12 km was not enough to beat Runner A's disciplined, consistent pace.
slo.safetyNotes: No specific hazards. Ensure learners use rulers carefully when drawing axes and constructing lines on graph paper.

LESSONS.overview:
This lesson marks a pivotal moment in the storyline sequence: learners have already calculated velocity and acceleration numerically (Lessons 1–2) and mastered displacement-time graphs (Lessons 3–4). Now they encounter a new type of graph — the velocity-time graph — which makes acceleration visible as the slope of a line rather than a single calculated number. The lesson is anchored in three complementary contexts: the 2023 Nairobi Marathon split-finish data (the anchoring phenomenon), a supporting ball-on-a-ramp scenario introduced briefly to provide a controlled physical reference, and a matatu journey on the Nakuru–Nairobi highway that provides a rich three-phase scenario (accelerating from a bus stop, cruising at constant speed, braking before Nakuru town) perfectly suited to constructing a multi-segment velocity-time graph.

Learners begin by predicting what a velocity-time graph for the matatu scenario would look like before they see any data, drawing on their intuitive understanding of motion and their prior work with displacement-time graphs. They then receive a printed data table for the matatu journey and construct the graph in pairs, identifying each segment's gradient and labelling it as acceleration or deceleration. The Explain phase connects the graph shape back to the marathon: Runner B's split data is re-examined as a velocity-time sketch, making viscerally clear how Runner B's steep positive gradient (sprint acceleration) in the final kilometres came too late to overcome Runner A's consistent, flat velocity profile over the whole race.

Throughout the lesson, the teacher uses targeted cold-calling, structured wait time, and a segment-annotation routine to build precision in mathematical language. By the end of the lesson, every learner should be able to state that the gradient of a velocity-time graph equals acceleration, sketch the three characteristic segment shapes (rising line, horizontal line, falling line), and connect these shapes to the real motion of runners and vehicles they know from their daily lives in Kenya.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners are presented with a written scenario — no numbers yet — describing a matatu leaving a bus stop on Uhuru Highway in Nairobi: it starts from rest, builds up speed over 10 seconds, travels at a steady speed for 30 seconds, then slows down and stops at the next stage. Each learner individually sketches what they think the velocity-time graph for this journey would look like on a blank axes grid in their exercise books, labelling the three phases. They write one sentence beneath the sketch predicting what the slope of each section will look like and what that slope might mean.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the matatu scenario on the board (written in large text or on a manila card). Say: 'Before we look at any numbers, I want you to think about what is actually happening to the matatu's speed at each stage of this journey. In your exercise books, sketch what you think a velocity-time graph would look like — velocity on the y-axis, time on the x-axis. You have 3 minutes working silently and individually.' Start a visible timer. After 3 minutes, say: 'Now look at your sketch. Under it, write ONE sentence describing what the slope of each section means about the matatu's motion.' Allow a further 2 minutes. After 5 minutes total, cold-call 3 learners to describe their sketches aloud — choose one learner whose sketch shows all three phases correctly, one who has the acceleration phase correct but the deceleration phase flat, and one who has drawn a straight diagonal line the whole way. For each, ask: 'What did you decide to do with the line during the steady-speed phase? Why?' Apply a minimum 12-second wait time after each question before accepting an answer. Do NOT correct errors yet — note the range of predictions on the board as three labelled sketches titled 'Prediction A', 'Prediction B', 'Prediction C' to return to in the Explain phase.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Activate-and-Anchor Prediction: By committing to a sketch before seeing data, learners activate prior knowledge from displacement-time graphs (Lessons 3–4) and create a cognitive 'hook' that makes the subsequent data observation more meaningful. Recording predictions publicly creates accountability and a reference point for revision, embodying the NGSS Science and Engineering Practice of developing and using models.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher circulates during the 5-minute prediction window and looks for three indicators: (1) Does the learner start the graph at v = 0 (matatu begins from rest)? (2) Does the learner draw a rising line, a horizontal line, and a falling line — or some other combination? (3) Does the learner's written sentence use the word 'slope', 'gradient', 'speed', or 'acceleration' in a mathematically meaningful way? Learners who draw a horizontal line throughout have not yet transferred gradient-as-rate from displacement-time graphs — the teacher notes their names and targets them during Observe Phase pair work.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners receive a printed data table (or copy it from the board) showing the velocity of the matatu at regular time intervals during its journey from the Kencom bus stop on Moi Avenue, Nairobi. The table shows: t = 0 s, v = 0 m/s; t = 2 s, v = 3 m/s; t = 4 s, v = 6 m/s; t = 6 s, v = 9 m/s; t = 8 s, v = 12 m/s; t = 10 s, v = 15 m/s; t = 20 s, v = 15 m/s; t = 30 s, v = 15 m/s; t = 40 s, v = 15 m/s; t = 46 s, v = 9 m/s; t = 52 s, v = 3 m/s; t = 55 s, v = 0 m/s. Working in pairs, learners plot these points on graph paper using a provided scale (x-axis: 1 cm = 5 s; y-axis: 1 cm = 3 m/s), draw straight lines connecting points within each segment, and label the three phases: 'Phase 1: Accelerating', 'Phase 2: Constant velocity', 'Phase 3: Decelerating'. They then calculate the gradient of Phase 1 and Phase 3 using rise-over-run and record the values with units.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute graph paper and the data table simultaneously. Say: 'You are going to construct a velocity-time graph for this matatu journey. Work in pairs. Step one — decide on your scale and label your axes with units. Step two — plot every point in the table. Step three — draw straight lines connecting points within each of the three phases. Step four — label the three phases. You have 10 minutes.' Circulate actively. At the 4-minute mark, pause the class for 30 seconds and say: 'Quick check — raise your hand if you have already labelled both axes with the correct units. Good. If you haven't, do that now before plotting any more points — units are not optional in mathematics.' At the 8-minute mark, when most pairs have completed the graph, say: 'Now, without touching your calculator, estimate the gradient of Phase 1. Talk to your partner for 30 seconds.' After 30 seconds, cold-call 2 pairs: 'Pair at the back — what gradient did you estimate for Phase 1, and how did you calculate it?' Apply 12-second wait time. Then cold-call a second pair: 'Do you agree? What value did you get, and what are the units of this gradient?' Confirm on the board: gradient of Phase 1 = (15 − 0) ÷ (10 − 0) = 1.5 m/s². Write clearly: 'Gradient of v-t graph = acceleration (m/s²).' Repeat the gradient calculation routine for Phase 3 with a third cold-call pair.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data-to-Graph Construction with Segment Annotation: Learners do not merely observe a pre-drawn graph — they construct it from raw data, which deepens understanding of what each plotted point represents. The segment-annotation routine (labelling phases, calculating gradients) is a disciplined sensemaking practice that connects visual shape to numerical meaning, enacting the NGSS practice of Analysing and Interpreting Data. The pair structure ensures peer scaffolding during the technical plotting task.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher checks three specific quality indicators while circulating: (1) Are axes labelled with both quantity name AND units (e.g., 'Velocity (m/s)' and 'Time (s)')? — this is a non-negotiable mathematical standard. (2) Are points plotted accurately and connected with a ruler (straight-line segments, not a freehand curve)? (3) Is the gradient calculation set out as Δv/Δt with correct units of m/s²? Pairs who attempt to draw a smooth curve through all points have confused velocity-time with displacement-time graph conventions — teacher intervenes immediately with: 'Each segment represents a different type of motion. Should they be curves or straight lines? Why?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners engage in a structured whole-class discussion guided by three focus questions written on the board. First, they compare their completed velocity-time graph with the three 'Prediction' sketches saved from the Predict phase — identifying which prediction was most accurate and why. Second, they apply their gradient-calculation skill to a new context: the teacher displays a simplified velocity-time sketch for Runner B at the 2023 Nairobi Marathon (derived from the split-time data introduced in Lesson 1), showing Runner B's velocity dropping from approximately 5.8 m/s to 4.9 m/s between km 20 and km 30, then surging back to 6.2 m/s between km 30 and km 42. Learners calculate the gradient (acceleration) for each segment and annotate their marathon data sheet. Third, learners write a two-sentence explanation in their exercise books: 'The gradient of a velocity-time graph tells us ___. This explains what happened to Runner B between km 30 and km 42 because ___.'
framework.teacherMoves: Return to the three prediction sketches on the board. Say: 'Look at Prediction A, B, and C. Your real graph is now in front of you. Which prediction was closest to the truth — and more importantly, which part of the prediction was wrong and why?' Cold-call the learner whose sketch was used for 'Prediction C' (the straight diagonal line): 'Looking at your prediction now, what would a straight diagonal line across the whole graph have meant about the matatu's motion?' Apply 15-second wait time. Accept and build on the answer. Then transition: 'We have been thinking about a matatu. Let us go back to our marathon.' Project or draw the Runner B velocity-time sketch on the board. Say: 'This is a velocity-time sketch for Runner B, constructed from the split-time data we have been using since Lesson 1. I want you to calculate the gradient between km 30 and km 42 — remember, time values are on the x-axis. Work individually for 3 minutes.' After 3 minutes, cold-call 2 learners for their gradient values and units. Write: 'Runner B's acceleration in the final sprint = +0.027 m/s².' Then ask: 'If Runner B was accelerating, why did Runner A still win?' Apply 15-second wait time. Cold-call 3 learners. Guide toward: 'Because Runner B's average velocity over the full race was lower — the gradient being positive in the last section does not undo the low velocity in the middle section.' Conclude by having all learners complete the two-sentence written explanation in their books.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) Closure with Phenomenon Reconnection: Returning to the saved predictions makes the Explain phase a genuine revision of thinking rather than a passive reception of information. The two-sentence written explanation is a 'language frame' sensemaking strategy — the sentence stems require learners to state the mathematical principle AND connect it explicitly to the anchoring phenomenon, practising the NGSS Science and Engineering Practice of Constructing Explanations. Writing individually after whole-class discussion ensures every learner consolidates the idea in their own words.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher collects or scans (walks around to read) the two-sentence written explanations. Look for three quality indicators: (1) The first sentence correctly names gradient as acceleration and states the unit (m/s²). (2) The second sentence correctly identifies that Runner B's sprint acceleration in the final 12 km was positive but that his overall velocity profile was lower than Runner A's. (3) The explanation uses at least one number from the graph (e.g., a specific gradient value or velocity). Learners whose second sentence merely says 'Runner B was fast at the end' without mathematical reference have not yet connected the graph shape to the quantitative explanation — teacher flags these for targeted follow-up in the DQB phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the class Driving Question Board displayed at the front of the room. Each pair is given one sticky note (or writes in a designated DQB section of their exercise book if sticky notes are unavailable). They write one of three things: (a) a new question that today's lesson has raised for them about velocity-time graphs or acceleration, (b) a claim they can now make confidently about the marathon phenomenon with supporting evidence from today's graph work, or (c) a connection between today's lesson and a real-world Kenyan context beyond the marathon (e.g., a boda boda accelerating from a junction in Kisumu, a train leaving Nairobi terminus, a boat on Lake Victoria). Pairs share their sticky note contribution with the class in a 3-minute rapid round before placing it on the board.
framework.teacherMoves: Direct learners' attention to the DQB. Say: 'Our driving question asks: how can we use mathematics — calculations AND graphs — to fully describe the motion of any moving body? In Lessons 3 and 4 we answered part of this question using displacement-time graphs. Today we have added a second mathematical tool. I want you to think: what can we now say, and what can we still NOT yet say?' Distribute sticky notes or direct learners to the DQB section of their books. Say: 'With your partner, decide whether you are adding a NEW QUESTION, a CONFIDENT CLAIM, or a NEW CONNECTION. You have 2 minutes to write it.' After 2 minutes, do a rapid round: each pair reads their contribution aloud in one sentence — no more. Teacher organises contributions into three columns on the DQB as they are shared: 'We can now explain…', 'We still wonder…', 'New connections'. After the round, highlight two or three 'We still wonder' questions that will be addressed in Lesson 6 (interpreting velocity-time graphs: area under the graph as distance). Say: 'Hold onto these questions — they are exactly what we will attack next lesson.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Question Board Sorting: Organising learner contributions into 'can explain', 'still wonder', and 'new connections' columns makes the structure of scientific reasoning visible — learners see that good mathematics learning generates new questions as well as answers. This strategy enacts the NGSS practice of Engaging in Argument from Evidence by requiring learners to distinguish between claims they can support with today's graph evidence and genuine open questions. The public display maintains a cumulative record of the class's growing understanding across the eight-lesson sequence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher scans the sticky notes / written DQB contributions for two indicators: (1) Are 'confident claims' genuinely supported by evidence from today's work (e.g., 'We can calculate Runner B's acceleration in the sprint finish as +0.027 m/s² from the gradient of the velocity-time graph') rather than vague statements? (2) Are 'new questions' mathematically productive — pointing toward content still to come (e.g., 'Can we find the total distance from a velocity-time graph?') rather than off-topic? Vague claims or absent questions signal that the learner has not yet consolidated the lesson's core idea and need individual follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners retrieve their cumulative motion model — the annotated sketch or diagram of the marathon race that they have been building and revising since Lesson 1. Today they add a new layer: alongside their existing displacement-time graph sketches for Runner A and Runner B (constructed in Lesson 3), they now add small velocity-time sketch graphs for each runner, drawn directly beneath the corresponding displacement-time graph so the two graph types are vertically aligned for the same time axis. Learners annotate the velocity-time sketches with at least two gradient calculations (one acceleration, one deceleration) and write a two-phrase caption: 'Displacement-time graph shows… Velocity-time graph shows…' They also add an arrow labelled 'Runner A wins because…' connecting the two velocity-time sketches, completing in words and numbers why Runner A's flatter, more consistent velocity-time profile produced a lower total time despite Runner B's higher peak velocity.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Get out your cumulative marathon model from your folder or the back of your exercise book. You have been building this since Lesson 1. Today we are adding a second layer of graph evidence.' Write on the board: 'Task: Add velocity-time sketches for Runner A and Runner B. Annotate with at least 2 gradient calculations. Write the caption: Displacement-time graph shows ___ / Velocity-time graph shows ___. Add the arrow: Runner A wins because ___.' Allow 5 minutes for individual model revision. Circulate and look specifically at the arrow annotation. After 5 minutes, cold-call 2 learners to read their 'Runner A wins because…' sentence aloud. Apply 12-second wait time after each. If a learner says only 'because he was faster', probe: 'Faster where? At which kilometre? What does the gradient of his velocity-time graph tell us about his acceleration compared to Runner B?' Conclude the lesson by saying: 'Your model now has two types of graph for the same motion. Next lesson we will discover a third piece of information hidden in the velocity-time graph — the area under the line. Think about what that might represent before our next class.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision with Dual-Graph Alignment: Placing the velocity-time graph directly beneath the displacement-time graph for the same time axis is a disciplined representational strategy that builds multi-representational fluency — a core competency in the KICD curriculum. The vertical alignment makes visible the relationship between position, velocity, and acceleration in a single visual structure, enacting the NGSS practice of Developing and Using Models. The 'Runner A wins because…' annotation requires learners to synthesise all five lessons' worth of learning into a single evidence-based claim.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher checks three model-quality indicators: (1) Are the velocity-time sketches drawn on a correctly labelled set of axes (velocity vs. time, not distance vs. time)? (2) Do the gradient annotations include both a numerical value and the unit m/s² (not just a slope description)? (3) Does the 'Runner A wins because…' sentence reference the velocity-time graph specifically — i.e., does it mention gradient, average velocity, or a specific segment — rather than restating the finishing time alone? Models that lack numerical gradient annotations are flagged: the learner has grasped the visual concept but not yet the quantitative skill, which is the target outcome of Lesson 5.

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
1. During the Predict phase, how many learners spontaneously drew three distinct segments (rising, horizontal, falling) versus a single diagonal line — and what does this distribution tell me about how well the displacement-time graph work from Lessons 3 and 4 transferred to the new graph type?
2. When learners calculated the gradient of Phase 1 of the matatu graph, did they correctly attach the unit m/s² without prompting, or did they omit units or write m/s? What targeted intervention will I use at the start of Lesson 6 to address unit precision?
3. In the Explain phase, how many learners' two-sentence written explanations connected Runner B's positive gradient in the sprint finish to his overall lower average velocity — versus those who simply described the shape of the graph without a quantitative claim? What does this tell me about the depth of understanding of the relationship between local gradient and overall motion?
4. Reviewing the DQB contributions, how many pairs generated a 'new question' that points toward the area-under-the-graph concept (e.g., 'Can we find distance from a velocity-time graph?')? If fewer than one-third of pairs reached this question independently, how will I bridge to that concept at the start of Lesson 6?
5. In the Model Building phase, did learners' vertical alignment of displacement-time and velocity-time graphs reveal any misconceptions about the relationship between the two — for example, did any learner draw the velocity-time graph with the same shape as the displacement-time graph? How will I address this misconception before Lesson 6?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners observed that a velocity-time graph for a matatu journey on Uhuru Highway, Nairobi, produces three visually distinct segments: a rising straight line (acceleration from the Kencom bus stop), a horizontal straight line (constant cruising velocity), and a falling straight line (braking before the next stage). They also observed Runner B's velocity-time sketch derived from marathon split data, showing a mid-race dip in velocity followed by a steep positive gradient in the final 12 km sprint.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The gradient of a velocity-time graph equals acceleration (a = Δv/Δt, measured in m/s²). A horizontal segment means zero acceleration (constant velocity); a positive gradient means the object is speeding up; a negative gradient means it is decelerating. The shape of the velocity-time graph — its slopes, not just its start and end points — quantifies how rapidly velocity is changing at every moment of the journey.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The velocity-time graph of the Nairobi Marathon now mathematically explains what the split-time tables could only hint at: Runner B's steep positive gradient between km 30 and km 42 confirms a genuine sprint-finish acceleration, but the graph also shows that his velocity during km 20–30 was significantly lower than Runner A's flat, consistent velocity profile across the same period. The gradient calculations make it possible to state, with numbers and units, exactly how much Runner B accelerated — and why, despite that acceleration, his overall average velocity was lower, giving Runner A the victory.

LESSONS.title: Interpreting Velocity-Time Graphs: Area Under the Graph as Distance

slo.purpose: To enable learners to draw, read, and interpret velocity-time graphs, extract acceleration and deceleration from gradient, and calculate total distance travelled using area under the graph (counting squares, trapezium rule, and rectangle method) — connecting these skills to explain why Runner B lost the 2023 Nairobi Marathon despite leading at 30 km.
slo.knowledge: Learners will know that: (i) the gradient of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration (positive gradient) or deceleration (negative gradient); (ii) a horizontal segment on a velocity-time graph represents constant velocity and zero acceleration; (iii) the area under a velocity-time graph equals total distance (displacement) travelled; (iv) area can be calculated by counting grid squares or by decomposing regions into rectangles and trapeziums.
slo.skills: Learners will be able to: (i) draw a velocity-time graph from a given data table; (ii) calculate acceleration and deceleration from the gradient of line segments; (iii) calculate total distance travelled by finding the area under the graph using rectangles, trapeziums, and square-counting; (iv) compare the distance covered by two moving bodies in the same time interval using their velocity-time graphs.
slo.attitudes: Learners will: (i) appreciate that a graph shape — not just start and end points — tells the full story of motion; (ii) show integrity when reading values accurately from graphs; (iii) collaborate responsibly in group calculations; (iv) connect mathematical tools to real-life Kenyan contexts such as marathon running, matatu journeys, and SGR train travel.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we use velocity-time graphs?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 4–5 learners mastered displacement-time graphs and average speed. Lesson 6 introduces the velocity-time graph as the next evidence layer: learners discover that the shape of Runner B's velocity-time graph — specifically the area lost under the curve in the final 12 km — mathematically explains why Runner A overtook and won. This lesson directly resolves the central puzzle of the phenomenon and equips learners to update the Driving Question Board entry for 'How do we use velocity-time graphs?'
slo.safetyNotes: No physical hazards. Learners use rulers and pencils on graph paper; remind them to handle geometrical sets carefully. Ensure adequate spacing between desks during group work to prevent crowding.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin by predicting what a velocity-time graph for each marathon runner might look like, sketching rough curves from intuition. They then receive printed velocity-time data tables for two real-world Kenyan contexts — an SGR Madaraka Express journey (Nairobi–Mombasa segment) and a 400 m school race at Nakuru High School — and plot and interpret these graphs carefully. Through guided sensemaking, learners discover how to extract acceleration from gradient and total distance from area under the graph using rectangles, trapeziums, and square-counting. They apply this understanding retrospectively to Runner A and Runner B's velocity-time graphs, computing the area under each curve for the final 12 km to prove mathematically why Runner B lost. The lesson closes with a DQB update and a revised cumulative model showing velocity-time graphs as a third motion-description tool alongside distance-time and displacement-time graphs.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners receive a blank velocity-time axes (velocity on y-axis, time on x-axis) and the verbal description of Runner A and Runner B from the phenomenon. Working individually for 4 minutes, they sketch what they think each runner's velocity-time graph looks like — no calculation, pure intuition. They annotate their sketches with labels such as 'sprinting here', 'slowing at water station', 'steady pace'. They then share with a shoulder partner and note one similarity and one difference between their two sketches. A class gallery of 6 volunteer sketches is posted on the board for reference throughout the lesson.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute blank axes. Say: 'Before we do any maths, I want you to draw what you think Runner A and Runner B's velocity-time graphs look like — use what you already know about their race from Lesson 1. You have 4 minutes. Work alone first.' [START TIMER. Circulate silently for 2 minutes, noting misconceptions — e.g. learners drawing horizontal lines for both runners, or confusing velocity-time with displacement-time shape.] After 4 minutes: 'Turn to your shoulder partner. Tell them: one thing your graphs have in common, and one thing that is different. You have 90 seconds.' [WAIT. Circulate.] Cold-call 3 pairs to share. Probe: 'Why did you make Runner B's graph go higher at the start?' and 'What does a flat line on a velocity-time graph mean — is the runner stopped or moving at steady speed?' [WAIT TIME: 12 seconds after each question before taking responses.] Post 6 volunteer sketches on the board. Say: 'We will come back to these at the end of the lesson to see who was closest.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Elicitation of Prior Knowledge (Predict-first protocol): By committing a sketch to paper before instruction, learners activate and externalise their intuitive models of velocity change. This surfaces misconceptions — particularly confusion between the shape of a displacement-time graph and a velocity-time graph — so the teacher can address them explicitly during the Observe phase. The shoulder-partner share encourages learners to articulate their reasoning, deepening initial engagement with the phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher circulates and looks for: (i) learners who draw a horizontal line for both runners — indicates confusion between constant position and constant velocity; (ii) learners who draw Runner B's graph as continuously descending — indicates confusion between deceleration and negative velocity; (iii) learners who draw the y-axis as 'distance' — indicates prior lesson vocabulary has not consolidated. These learners are targeted for proximity support during Phase 2.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in groups of four to plot and read two velocity-time graphs from printed data tables. GRAPH 1 — SGR Madaraka Express (Nairobi to Athi River segment, approximately 30 minutes): the table gives velocity in km/h at 5-minute intervals: 0, 60, 120, 150, 150, 150, 130, 90, 0. Learners plot this on a 1 cm = 10 minutes (x) and 1 cm = 20 km/h (y) grid. GRAPH 2 — 400 m school race at Nakuru High School: the table gives velocity in m/s at 2-second intervals over 60 seconds for two athletes, Athlete Achieng (steady pace) and Athlete Kamau (fast start, tires midway, sprints last 10 s). Learners plot both athletes on the same axes using different colours. From each graph learners complete a structured observation worksheet: (a) identify and label phases — acceleration, constant velocity, deceleration; (b) describe the shape of the graph during each phase; (c) record the steepness (gradient) of the acceleration and deceleration segments; (d) describe what is happening to the moving body during each phase in plain language. Groups record observations on A3 paper for sharing.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute data tables, graph paper, and observation worksheets. Say: 'In your groups you are going to plot two real velocity-time graphs — one for the SGR train on its way out of Nairobi, and one for two athletes in a 400 m race at Nakuru High School. Plot carefully — use a ruler, label your axes with units, and give each graph a title.' [Allow 12 minutes for plotting. Circulate and check: axes labelled with units, correct scale chosen, points joined with straight lines between consecutive points — not curves — for this piecewise linear data.] After plotting, say: 'Now fill in your observation worksheet. For each graph, identify the phases and describe the shape. Do not calculate yet — just describe what you see.' [Allow 6 minutes.] After worksheets are partially completed, pause the class. Cold-call one group: 'What shape is the SGR graph during the first 10 minutes — and what is the train doing during that time?' [WAIT TIME: 12 seconds.] Cold-call a second group: 'On the Nakuru race graph, whose line is steeper at the start — Achieng's or Kamau's — and what does that steepness tell us?' [WAIT TIME: 12 seconds.] Affirm and clarify: 'A steeper slope on a velocity-time graph means velocity is changing faster — that means greater acceleration or greater deceleration.' Write this on the board as a class anchor statement.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data-to-Graph Translation (Structured Observation): Physically plotting data points and joining them forces learners to engage with each value in the table, making the shape of motion visible rather than abstract. The two-context design (train journey and athletics race) provides redundancy — if a learner does not connect with one context, the other reinforces the same concept. The structured observation worksheet scaffolds attention to phases of motion before any calculation, building the conceptual vocabulary (acceleration phase, constant velocity phase, deceleration phase) needed for Phase 3 sensemaking.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher checks for: (i) correctly labelled axes with units (velocity in km/h or m/s on y-axis; time on x-axis) — a missing unit is flagged immediately; (ii) straight-line segments drawn between data points (not freehand curves) — groups drawing smooth curves are redirected: 'We join consecutive data points with straight lines because we have data only at those intervals'; (iii) observation worksheet entries that use the words 'acceleration', 'constant', and 'deceleration' correctly in context — groups using vague language ('going fast', 'slowing') are prompted: 'Can you use the word acceleration or deceleration in that sentence?'

framework.learnerExperience: The class reconvenes for direct instruction and guided practice in two parts. PART A — Gradient = Acceleration: The teacher demonstrates on the SGR graph (drawn large on the board) how to calculate the gradient of the acceleration phase: gradient = change in velocity ÷ change in time = (120 − 0) km/h ÷ (10 − 0) min, converted to m/s². Learners calculate the deceleration phase gradient independently, then check with their group. They confirm that a negative gradient means deceleration. PART B — Area Under Graph = Distance: The teacher introduces the key concept: 'The area of the region between the velocity-time graph and the time axis equals the total distance travelled.' The teacher works through the SGR graph, decomposing it into recognisable shapes: a triangle (acceleration phase), two rectangles (constant velocity phase), and a trapezium (deceleration phase), and calculates area for each. Learners then independently calculate the total area under Athlete Kamau's velocity-time graph for the Nakuru 400 m race, using both shape decomposition and square-counting as a check. Finally, the teacher presents a simplified version of the Runner A vs Runner B velocity-time graph for the final 12 km of the Nairobi Marathon. Learners calculate the area under each curve for this segment. The calculation reveals that Runner B's area (distance covered) in the final 12 km is smaller than Runner A's — proving mathematically that Runner A overtook Runner B in the final stretch even though they covered the same total 42 km race distance.
framework.teacherMoves: PART A: Draw the SGR velocity-time graph large on the board. Say: 'The gradient of a velocity-time graph tells us how fast velocity is changing — that is acceleration. Watch how I calculate the gradient for the acceleration phase.' [Model calculation step by step, writing units at every step.] Say: 'Now you calculate the gradient of the deceleration phase — the segment where the train slows to zero. Work individually, then compare with your group. You have 3 minutes.' [WAIT. Circulate. After 3 minutes, cold-call 2 learners — choose one confident and one who appeared uncertain during circulation — to share their answers.] [WAIT TIME: 12 seconds between nomination and response.] Correct errors. Write on board: 'Gradient of velocity-time graph = acceleration (m/s²). Positive gradient = acceleration. Negative gradient = deceleration. Zero gradient = constant velocity.' PART B: Say: 'Now the big idea of today's lesson. Look at the SGR graph. The area of the region under the graph — between the line and the time axis — equals the total distance the train travelled. Let me show you how to find it by breaking the shape into pieces we know.' [Decompose into triangle, rectangles, trapezium. Calculate each. Sum them.] Say: 'Now use the same method to find the total distance Athlete Kamau ran. Use shape decomposition first, then count squares to check. You have 8 minutes.' [Circulate actively. Prompt groups who are stuck: 'What shapes can you see when you look at the graph?'] Cold-call one group to present their answer and method on the board. [WAIT TIME after each board explanation: 10 seconds for peer questions.] MARATHON APPLICATION: Display the simplified Runner A vs Runner B velocity-time graph for km 30–42. Say: 'Calculate the area under Runner A's line for this final 12 km segment. Then calculate the area under Runner B's line. What do you notice?' [Allow 6 minutes.] Cold-call 2 groups. Say: 'So — mathematically — who covered more distance in the final 12 km? Why did Runner A win?' [WAIT TIME: 15 seconds. Expect: 'Runner A covered more distance in the final 12 km because the area under Runner A's graph is larger, meaning Runner A's velocity was higher for longer.']
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Shape Decomposition and Area Calculation (Quantitative Sensemaking): Decomposing the area under a velocity-time graph into triangles, rectangles, and trapeziums connects new content (area as distance) to prior geometric knowledge, making the concept accessible. The deliberate pairing of shape-decomposition and square-counting as independent verification methods builds mathematical confidence and self-checking habits. The marathon application at the end of Phase 3 creates a direct, emotionally resonant payoff — the same Kenyan athletes learners have been tracking since Lesson 1 — making the abstract area calculation meaningful and memorable.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher checks for: (i) correct identification of shapes (triangle, rectangle, trapezium) within the graph region — learners who shade the entire rectangle up to the peak velocity are redirected to shade only to the line; (ii) correct formula application — trapezium area = ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × height, with correct identification of which dimensions are 'height' and which are 'parallel sides' in the context of the graph; (iii) correct units for area — velocity (m/s or km/h) × time (s or h) = distance (m or km) — learners who write 'm/s²' for the area answer are prompted: 'What are the units of the two axes? What do you get when you multiply them?'; (iv) the marathon comparison calculation: both area values computed and a clear written conclusion linking larger area to greater distance covered.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups spend 6 minutes updating the class Driving Question Board. Each group receives three sticky notes in different colours: ORANGE — 'What we can now answer'; GREEN — 'New questions this lesson raised'; PURPLE — 'What we still need to find out to fully answer the driving question'. Groups add their notes to the DQB column labelled 'How do we use velocity-time graphs?' Representative answers expected on orange notes: 'We can find acceleration from the gradient'; 'We can find total distance from area under the graph'; 'We can prove Runner A won because the area under Runner A's graph in the final 12 km is bigger.' Green notes might include: 'What if the graph is curved — not straight lines?'; 'Can we use this for the matatu on Nakuru highway — does it have smooth acceleration or steps?'. The teacher reads selected notes aloud and facilitates a 3-minute whole-class discussion to consolidate. The teacher explicitly links back to the phenomenon: 'We now have a mathematical answer to our driving question — not just a description, but a calculation that proves what happened at every point in the race.'
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute sticky notes. Say: 'You have 6 minutes in your groups. On the ORANGE note write what from today's lesson you can now use to answer our driving question about the Nairobi Marathon runners. On the GREEN note write a new question today's lesson raised. On the PURPLE note write what we still do not know.' [Circulate. Prompt groups whose orange notes are vague — e.g. 'we learnt about graphs' — with: 'Can you be more specific? Which calculation did you do today that helps explain why Runner A won?'] After 6 minutes, cold-call 4 groups to read their orange notes. Write a class summary on the board: 'From v-t graphs we can find: (1) acceleration = gradient; (2) distance = area under graph.' Ask: 'Before today, could we have proved mathematically why Runner B lost? What did we need that we did not have in Lessons 4 and 5?' [WAIT TIME: 12 seconds.] Affirm: 'Exactly — we needed the velocity-time graph and the area calculation. That is today's contribution to the driving question.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board Protocol (Metacognitive Tracking): The three-colour sticky note system externalises the class's evolving understanding and makes thinking visible to all learners. The explicit distinction between 'what we can now answer' and 'what we still need' models scientific sensemaking — knowledge building is cumulative and iterative. Connecting the DQB update directly back to the marathon phenomenon reinforces that every lesson is a purposeful step toward resolving the anchoring puzzle, not an isolated skill exercise.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher reads all orange sticky notes before the lesson ends. Adequate orange notes should reference: gradient, acceleration, area, and distance. Notes that only reference 'drawing graphs' indicate learners have not yet consolidated the interpretive skills and will need targeted re-engagement in Lesson 7. Green and purple notes are photographed (or transcribed) to inform lesson planning for Lessons 7 and 8.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners individually update their cumulative motion model — a diagram they have been building since Lesson 1 to describe Runner A and Runner B's race. In Lessons 4–5 they added displacement-time graphs and speed calculations to the model. Today each learner adds: (i) a velocity-time graph sketch for each runner for the full race (labelling acceleration at the start, steady pace, water station slow-downs, and the final sprint); (ii) annotation arrows showing where gradient is steep (high acceleration) and shallow (slow acceleration); (iii) shaded regions on the final 12 km segment of each runner's graph with a written label: 'Area = distance covered in final 12 km. Runner A's area > Runner B's area. Therefore Runner A wins.' Learners write a 3-sentence model summary at the bottom: 'A velocity-time graph shows how velocity changes with time. The gradient of any segment tells us the acceleration or deceleration at that point. The area under the graph tells us the total distance travelled — and this is why Runner A, who had a higher velocity for longer in the final 12 km, overtook Runner B and won the 2023 Nairobi Marathon.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Get out your cumulative model from Lessons 1 to 5. Today you are going to add the velocity-time graph layer. I want you to sketch the velocity-time graph for each runner for the full race — label all phases. Then shade the final 12 km section on each runner's graph and write the area comparison. Finally, write your 3-sentence model summary. You have 8 minutes.' [Circulate. Look for: correct graph orientation (velocity on y-axis); correct labelling of phases; shaded region clearly marked; written comparison present.] With 2 minutes remaining: 'Swap your model with someone not in your group. Check: does their velocity-time graph correctly show Runner B starting faster? Does it show Runner A pulling ahead in the final section? Does their 3-sentence summary mention gradient AND area? Give one piece of specific written feedback.' [Allow 2 minutes for peer feedback.] Close: 'Hold up your model. Look at how much it has grown since Lesson 1 — we started with split times and a question. Now we have a mathematical proof. In Lesson 7 we will use what we know about velocity-time graphs to calculate relative speed — for example, when a matatu on the Nakuru highway overtakes a lorry.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision (Progressive Model Building): Adding the velocity-time graph layer to an existing model — rather than starting fresh — makes the accumulation of knowledge physically visible and conceptually coherent. Learners can literally see the displacement-time graph (from Lesson 5) sitting beside the velocity-time graph (from today), reinforcing that these are complementary descriptions of the same event. The peer-feedback protocol (checking for gradient label AND area label) operationalises the lesson's two key learning outcomes and gives every learner one last retrieval opportunity before the lesson ends.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher collects or photographs 6–8 models (stratified by ability group) to review before Lesson 7. Success criteria checked: (i) velocity-time graph present with velocity on y-axis and time on x-axis; (ii) at least two phases labelled (e.g. acceleration, constant velocity, deceleration); (iii) final 12 km shaded on both runners' graphs; (iv) written area comparison present and correct in direction (Runner A area > Runner B area); (v) 3-sentence summary references both gradient (acceleration) and area (distance). Learners with fewer than 3 of 5 criteria met are flagged for a 5-minute catch-up at the start of Lesson 7.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following: (1) GRADIENT CALCULATION — Were learners able to correctly identify the rise (change in velocity) and run (change in time) on the SGR graph? Did they apply correct units (m/s² or km/h per minute)? If many learners wrote incorrect units, plan a 5-minute unit analysis warm-up at the start of Lesson 7. (2) AREA DECOMPOSITION — Which shape caused the most difficulty — the triangle, the rectangle, or the trapezium? If the trapezium caused widespread errors, prepare an additional worked example using a matatu velocity-time graph at the start of Lesson 7. (3) MARATHON CONNECTION — Did learners independently articulate, in Phase 4, that Runner A won because of greater area under the graph in the final 12 km? If this connection required significant teacher scaffolding, consider whether the phenomenon data (Runner A and Runner B velocity tables) needs to be made more concrete — e.g. providing numerical velocity values for each 5 km split rather than a qualitative description. (4) DQB ENGAGEMENT — Were green sticky notes (new questions) substantive and forward-looking (e.g. 'What if the graph is curved?')? Substantive green notes indicate high-level engagement and should be celebrated and used to frame Lesson 7. Superficial green notes ('I want to know more about graphs') indicate learners are not yet connecting the DQB to the driving question — revisit the DQB protocol briefly at the start of Lesson 7. (5) EQUITY MONITOR — Did all four members of each group contribute to the graph plotting and area calculation, or did one learner dominate? If group dynamics were unequal, restructure groups for Lesson 7 or assign specific roles (Plotter, Calculator, Recorder, Presenter) from the outset.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners plotted and examined velocity-time graphs for two Kenyan real-world contexts: the SGR Madaraka Express journey out of Nairobi and a 400 m athletics race at Nakuru High School. They identified and labelled three motion phases — acceleration, constant velocity, and deceleration — by observing the shape and slope of each graph segment. They also observed a simplified velocity-time graph comparing Runner A and Runner B's motion in the final 12 km of the 2023 Nairobi Marathon.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Learners learned that: (i) the gradient of a velocity-time graph equals acceleration — a steep positive gradient means rapid acceleration, a negative gradient means deceleration, and a zero gradient (horizontal line) means constant velocity; (ii) the area of the region between the velocity-time graph and the time axis equals the total distance (displacement) travelled; (iii) this area can be calculated by decomposing the region into rectangles and trapeziums, or by counting grid squares; (iv) comparing the areas under Runner A's and Runner B's velocity-time graphs for the final 12 km mathematically proves that Runner A covered more ground in that segment and therefore overtook Runner B to win the race.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Learners explained, using their area calculations, why Runner B lost the 2023 Nairobi Marathon despite leading at the 30 km mark: Runner B's velocity dropped significantly in the final 12 km (smaller area under the graph = less distance covered per unit time), while Runner A maintained a higher velocity for longer (larger area = more distance covered). This resolved the central puzzle of the phenomenon and directly answered the key inquiry question 'How do we use velocity-time graphs?' Learners updated their cumulative models and the Driving Question Board to reflect this mathematical explanation.

LESSONS.title: Relative Speed — Who Gets There First When Everyone Is Moving?
LESSONS.aresKeywords: relative speed, same direction, opposite directions, overtaking, linear motion Kenya

slo.purpose: Learners extend their understanding of motion from a single moving body to two bodies moving simultaneously, discovering that the speed one body appears to have depends entirely on the motion of the observer — and that this relative speed determines overtaking time, collision risk, and NTSA road-safety limits on Kenyan highways.
slo.knowledge:
• Define relative speed as the speed of one body as observed from another moving body.
• State and apply the two rules: relative speed of bodies moving in the SAME direction = difference of their speeds; relative speed of bodies moving in OPPOSITE directions = sum of their speeds.
• Solve problems involving time to overtake, time to meet, and distance apart using relative speed in Kenyan contexts (matatus on Nakuru highway, boats on Lake Victoria, runners on a track).
slo.skills:
• Calculate relative speed, time to meet, and time to overtake for two moving bodies given their individual speeds and initial separation.
• Interpret real-world road-safety data (NTSA speed limits) using the mathematics of relative speed to justify why high closing speeds are dangerous.
slo.attitudes:
• Appreciate that mathematics is a tool for protecting human life — the same equations used to explain Runner B overtaking Runner A also explain why head-on collisions on Kenyan highways are catastrophic.
• Show responsibility and integrity by recording calculations accurately and engaging honestly with road-safety implications.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we use mathematics — specifically relative speed — to describe what one moving body experiences when another moving body approaches or passes it?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1–6 built the complete mathematical toolkit for describing a SINGLE body in motion (distance, displacement, velocity, acceleration, displacement-time graphs, velocity-time graphs, and area under a graph). Lesson 7 now introduces the critical next layer: what happens when TWO bodies are moving at the same time? By using the matatu-overtaking supporting phenomenon — a matatu travelling at 90 km/h overtaking a bus travelling at 60 km/h on the Nakuru–Nairobi highway — learners discover that the speed each driver perceives the other to have is not their absolute speed but their RELATIVE speed. This bridges directly to the marathon phenomenon: Runner A appeared to 'fly past' Runner B in the final sprint not because Runner A suddenly ran 21 km/h, but because Runner B had slowed to 17 km/h, making the relative speed between them 4 km/h — the actual overtaking speed. Learners now have a complete quantitative explanation for every event in the 2023 Nairobi Marathon.
slo.safetyNotes: No specific physical hazards. When discussing road-safety contexts, ensure the conversation is sensitive — some learners may have been affected by road accidents. Frame discussion constructively around NTSA data and prevention, not graphic descriptions of crashes.

LESSONS.overview:
Lesson 7 is the penultimate evidence-gathering lesson in the sequence and marks the conceptual shift from single-body motion to two-body relative motion. Having spent Lessons 1–6 building a complete mathematical toolkit — velocity, acceleration, displacement-time graphs, velocity-time graphs, and the area-under-graph method for distance — learners are now ready to ask a more sophisticated question: what does motion look like from the perspective of another moving body? The lesson is anchored by a vivid supporting phenomenon: a matatu travelling at 90 km/h attempting to overtake a Mombasa-bound bus travelling at 60 km/h on the Nakuru–Nairobi highway. Students must first predict whether the matatu driver can safely complete the overtake before an oncoming car arrives, then work through the mathematics of relative speed to test their prediction.

The lesson introduces both cases of relative speed in a carefully sequenced order. Same-direction motion is treated first using the matatu-overtaking scenario: because both vehicles travel in the same direction, the matatu approaches the bus at only 30 km/h — its relative speed — not at 90 km/h. This explains why overtaking manoeuvres on Kenyan highways take far longer than inexperienced drivers expect, leading to the dangerous head-on collisions that NTSA statistics document every year. Opposite-direction motion is then explored using boats on Lake Victoria (a passenger ferry from Kisumu to Homa Bay meeting a cargo vessel travelling the opposite way) and runners on an athletics track. In the opposite-direction case the closing speed equals the SUM of the two speeds, which is why head-on crashes are so catastrophic.

Throughout the lesson learners connect back to the marathon anchoring phenomenon: Runner A's dramatic overtake of Runner B in the final 2 km is now fully explained not just by the velocity-time graph shapes from Lesson 6, but by the precise relative speed between the two athletes at that moment. The Driving Question Board is updated to show that the driving question is now answerable in full, setting up Lesson 8 as the synthesis and consolidation lesson.

framework.learnerExperience: Students are shown a short written scenario projected on the board (or read aloud): 'A matatu leaves Nakuru travelling towards Nairobi at 90 km/h. Exactly 0.5 km ahead on the same road, a bus is travelling in the same direction at 60 km/h. The matatu driver decides to overtake. An oncoming car is 3 km away, approaching at 100 km/h. Will the matatu complete the overtake safely before the oncoming car arrives?' Working individually in their exercise books, students write: (a) their gut-feel YES/NO answer, (b) one sentence explaining their reasoning, and (c) a numerical estimate of how long the overtake will take. Students are told not to worry about being right — this is about making their current thinking visible.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the scenario and say: 'Before we do any calculation, I want every single one of you to write your own answer — yes or no — and your reason. You have 2 minutes. No talking yet.' [WAIT 2 minutes, circulate and scan responses.] After 2 minutes: 'Keep your prediction visible — we will come back to it. Raise your hand if you said YES, the overtake is safe.' [Count hands, note number.] 'Raise your hand if you said NO.' [Count hands.] Cold-call 2 YES students and 2 NO students: 'Amina, walk us through your thinking in one sentence.' [WAIT 10 seconds after each response before calling the next student.] After four responses say: 'Interesting — we have disagreement in this room. That is exactly what good mathematics is for. Let us go find out who is right, and more importantly, WHY.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-before-observe (PBO) anchored to a Kenyan road scenario. By committing a prediction to paper before any instruction, every learner activates prior intuition about speed and creates a cognitive 'hook' — a genuine question they now want resolved. The public show-of-hands creates productive disagreement that motivates the observe phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher scans written predictions for two things: (1) whether students are comparing speeds or only thinking about one vehicle's speed (diagnostic of whether they already have any intuition about relative motion), and (2) whether any student has spontaneously written 'difference' or 'closing speed' — indicating prior knowledge. Record the class split (YES vs NO) on the board to revisit after the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Students work in pairs on a structured data-gathering activity using three carefully sequenced worked scenarios printed on a single A4 activity sheet (or copied from the board into exercise books). SCENARIO 1 (Same direction — the matatu): Matatu speed = 90 km/h; Bus speed = 60 km/h; Gap = 0.5 km. Students are told: 'From the matatu driver's seat, the bus is NOT stationary — it is moving away at 60 km/h. The matatu gains on the bus at a rate of (90 − 60) = 30 km/h. Use this closing speed to calculate how long it takes the matatu to cover the 0.5 km gap.' Students calculate time = 0.5 ÷ 30 hours = 1 minute. They then calculate how far the oncoming car travels in that same 1 minute at 100 km/h, and compare it to the 3 km gap. SCENARIO 2 (Opposite direction — Lake Victoria ferries): A passenger ferry leaves Kisumu at 25 km/h heading to Homa Bay. A cargo vessel leaves Homa Bay at 15 km/h heading to Kisumu. The ports are 60 km apart. Students use relative speed = 25 + 15 = 40 km/h to find when and where the vessels meet. SCENARIO 3 (Runners — connecting to the marathon): In the final 2 km of the Nairobi Marathon, Runner A is travelling at 21 km/h and Runner B (who is 200 m ahead) has slowed to 17 km/h. Students calculate the relative speed (4 km/h) and the time for Runner A to close the 200 m gap.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute/display the activity sheet and say: 'I am going to show you one key idea, and then you and your partner will apply it to all three scenarios.' Write on the board: 'SAME DIRECTION: Relative speed = Fast speed − Slow speed. OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS: Relative speed = Speed A + Speed B.' Say: 'This is the rule. Your job right now is not to memorise it — your job is to USE it on these three scenarios and see if the answers make sense to you.' [Allow 10 minutes of pair work. Circulate continuously.] After 5 minutes, pause the class: 'How many pairs have finished Scenario 1? Good. A quick check — cold-call: Juma, what closing speed did you get for the matatu and the bus?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] 'And Brian, does the matatu complete the overtake safely?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] After all three scenarios: 'Scenario 3 is the one I want you to think about most carefully. That is Runner A overtaking Runner B. Sound familiar?' [Pause 5 seconds — allow the connection to the marathon to land.] Cold-call one more pair: 'Fatuma, what is the relative speed of the two runners, and what does that number mean in plain language?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured Inquiry with Scaffolded Scenarios (graduated complexity). The three scenarios are deliberately sequenced: matatu-overtaking (same direction, danger context), Lake Victoria ferries (opposite direction, distance-to-meet), and marathon runners (same direction, connecting back to the anchoring phenomenon). Each scenario requires students to identify which rule to apply before calculating, building procedural fluency while simultaneously demanding conceptual reasoning about direction. Pair work ensures every student articulates thinking aloud, not just the fastest workers.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher listens for three specific misconceptions during circulation: (1) students adding speeds even in the same-direction case ('they are both fast, so add them') — redirect by asking 'from the matatu driver's window, is the bus getting CLOSER or FURTHER AWAY, and how FAST?'; (2) students forgetting to convert units (km/h to km/min or keeping consistent units) — check unit labels in working; (3) students who cannot connect Scenario 3 back to the marathon — prompt with 'Which runner is Runner A in our marathon story, and what was happening to Runner B's speed in the final 2 km according to the velocity-time graph we drew in Lesson 6?'

framework.learnerExperience: The class comes together for whole-group sensemaking. The teacher leads a structured discussion that formalises the two relative-speed rules, connects them to the NTSA road-safety context, and then returns to the original prediction to resolve it. Students annotate their activity sheets with formal definitions and mark whether their original predictions were correct. The class then works through two extension problems: (a) A piki-piki (motorcycle) travelling at 70 km/h is chased by a police car travelling at 110 km/h. They start 1.2 km apart. How long before the police car catches the motorcycle? (b) Two matatus leave Nairobi and Mombasa simultaneously, 480 km apart, travelling towards each other at 80 km/h and 100 km/h respectively. When and where do they meet? Students solve these in their exercise books, then a volunteer writes the solution on the board for class verification.
framework.teacherMoves: Begin by returning to the board prediction tally: 'At the start of the lesson, [X] of you said the overtake was safe and [Y] said it was not. Let us now use the mathematics to settle this.' Work through Scenario 1 on the board step by step, narrating each line: 'Step 1: Identify direction — same direction, so we SUBTRACT. Step 2: Relative speed = 90 − 60 = 30 km/h. Step 3: Time to close 0.5 km gap at 30 km/h = 0.5/30 hours = 1 minute. Step 4: In 1 minute, the oncoming car travels 100 × (1/60) = 1.67 km. Step 5: The oncoming car started 3 km away and has covered 1.67 km — it is now only 1.33 km away. So what is your verdict?' [WAIT 15 seconds, cold-call 2 students.] Then say: 'Now I want you to tell me WHY head-on collisions are so much more deadly than rear-end collisions. Use the words RELATIVE SPEED in your answer.' [WAIT 15 seconds.] Cold-call 3 students. Formalise: 'Head-on collision relative speed = 80 + 80 = 160 km/h. Rear-end: 90 − 60 = 30 km/h. The force of impact depends on this relative speed. That is why NTSA sets speed limits — it is not arbitrary, it is mathematics protecting lives.' For the extension problems, say: 'In your books — 3 minutes. Go.' [Circulate.] After 3 minutes: 'Wanjiku, come and write your solution for the police car problem. Everyone else, check your own work as she writes.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim–Evidence–Reasoning (CER) structured discussion. Teacher explicitly models the three-step CER pattern for each problem: CLAIM (state the answer), EVIDENCE (show the calculation), REASONING (explain why the rule applies — same direction subtract, opposite directions add). Students are required to use this same structure when explaining their extension-problem solutions. This is the same scientific-reasoning structure embedded throughout the ARES sequence and reinforces the habit of justifying answers, not just stating them.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher collects two observable indicators: (1) During the piki-piki problem, can students independently identify that same-direction subtraction applies without being prompted? (2) In the Nairobi–Mombasa matatu problem, can students correctly set up distance = relative speed × time AND then calculate where the meeting point is (not just when)? Students who can do both are at 'Meets Expectations'; students who also correctly interpret the road-safety implication in their own words are at 'Exceeds Expectations'. Students who confuse the two rules need targeted same-day intervention using the direction-of-motion visual (arrows on number line) drawn on a mini-whiteboard.

framework.learnerExperience: Students return to the class Driving Question Board displayed at the front of the room. They review all the sticky notes and annotations accumulated across Lessons 1–6. Working in their table groups (3–4 students), each group receives two sticky notes: one GREEN ('We can now answer this') and one ORANGE ('New question this lesson raised'). Groups discuss which existing DQB questions can now be fully answered using relative speed (e.g. 'How did Runner A overtake Runner B if they were both running at high speed?'), and write any new questions about real-world applications (e.g. 'Does the NTSA use relative speed equations to set speed limits?' or 'What happens to relative speed when one car brakes suddenly?'). Groups post their sticky notes and one spokesperson reads them aloud to the class.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take 3 minutes in your groups. Look at our DQB. Which questions can we NOW answer that we could not answer before Lesson 7? Write your answer on the GREEN note. Then think: did today's lesson raise a NEW question for you? Write it on the ORANGE note.' [WAIT 3 minutes. Circulate and prompt quiet groups: 'What about Runner A overtaking Runner B — could you explain that fully before today? Can you now?'] After groups post notes, go to the board and point to the driving question: 'How can we use mathematics — calculations and graphs — to FULLY describe and explain the motion of ANY moving body?' Cold-call one student: 'Otieno — after seven lessons, can we now answer this question? What is still missing?' [WAIT 15 seconds.] Acknowledge any remaining gaps (e.g. 'We have not yet done a full problem combining graphs AND relative speed for the marathon scenario — that is Lesson 8.') Say: 'Our DQB shows us we are almost there. One lesson to go.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board Annotation (Progressive Refinement). By colour-coding sticky notes as GREEN (resolved) and ORANGE (new questions), students experience the scientific process authentically: answering one question always generates new ones. This also provides the teacher with a real-time class-level formative snapshot of which concepts have genuinely landed versus which remain unclear, shaping the design of Lesson 8.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher photographs the DQB after the lesson. Key indicator: can at least 70% of groups correctly identify the Runner A / Runner B overtaking question as now answerable using relative speed? If groups are still posting this as an ORANGE (unresolved) note, it signals that the connection between Scenarios 1/3 and the marathon phenomenon was not made explicit enough and must be revisited in the opening of Lesson 8.

framework.learnerExperience: Each student returns to their cumulative 'Motion Model' — the annotated diagram they have been building since Lesson 1 that represents the complete story of the 2023 Nairobi Marathon using every mathematical tool learned so far. In Lesson 7, students add a NEW layer to their model: a two-body diagram showing the final 2 km of the race. They draw two parallel horizontal arrows (representing Runner A and Runner B moving in the same direction), label the arrows with the velocities from Lesson 6's velocity-time graph (Runner A: 21 km/h, Runner B: 17 km/h), write the relative speed calculation beside the diagram (21 − 17 = 4 km/h), and annotate the 200 m gap with the time calculation showing when Runner A catches Runner B. Below the diagram they write a one-sentence 'mathematical story' of the overtake in plain English, for example: 'From Runner B's perspective, Runner A appeared to be approaching at only 4 km/h — but that was enough to close the 200 m gap in 3 minutes and win the race.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your Motion Models. Today we add the final piece of the mathematical story of the marathon — the moment Runner A overtook Runner B. I want you to draw a two-body diagram. Use the velocity values from your velocity-time graph in Lesson 6.' [Display the relevant section of the Lesson 6 v-t graph on the board as a reference.] 'You have 4 minutes. Draw, calculate, annotate, and write your one-sentence story.' [WAIT 4 minutes, circulate and look at models.] After 4 minutes, cold-call one student to read their one-sentence story aloud. Ask the class: 'Is this a complete mathematical explanation of why Runner A won? What did we use from Lesson 1? Lesson 2? Lesson 3 and 4? Lesson 5 and 6? And now Lesson 7?' [WAIT 10 seconds between each lesson reference — students call out or raise hands.] Conclude: 'Your model now contains distance, displacement, velocity, acceleration, a displacement-time graph, a velocity-time graph, area under the graph for distance, AND relative speed. That is the complete mathematical toolkit for linear motion. In Lesson 8, we bring it all together.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision (Progressive Modelling). The running Motor Model that students have built across all seven lessons functions as a personalised scientific model in the NGSS sense: it is revised and extended each lesson as new evidence is gathered and new concepts are learned. Adding the two-body relative-speed layer in Lesson 7 makes the model 'complete' — every event in the marathon phenomenon now has a mathematical representation in the model. The one-sentence 'mathematical story' annotation develops scientific communication skills and forces students to translate symbolic mathematics into coherent English prose.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher collects (or photographs) 4–5 models from different ability groups. Check for three things: (1) correct identification of which runner is faster and correct application of the subtraction rule (not addition); (2) correct unit handling in the time calculation (converting km/h and km to find time in hours, then converting to minutes); (3) the one-sentence story accurately uses the phrase 'relative speed' or 'from Runner B's perspective' — indicating conceptual understanding, not just procedural calculation. Students whose models show correct calculation but incorrect prose (or no prose) are directed to the 'Tell Me the Story' prompt card: 'If Runner B could feel Runner A approaching, what speed would Runner A seem to be running at?'

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
1. When students worked through Scenario 1 (the matatu overtaking), were they able to independently identify that same-direction motion requires SUBTRACTION before I stated the rule, or did they wait for me to give the formula? What does this tell me about their readiness for Lesson 8's synthesis task?
2. Were the three scenarios sufficiently differentiated in difficulty and context? Did the Lake Victoria ferry scenario (Scenario 2) cause more confusion than the road scenarios — and if so, is it because the context was unfamiliar, or because the 'distance to meeting point' calculation added an extra step beyond what students were ready for?
3. When I asked students to explain WHY head-on collisions are more dangerous than rear-end collisions using the words 'relative speed', how many students gave a calculation-based answer versus a vague intuitive answer? This reveals whether the concept is conceptually understood or only procedurally applied.
4. Looking at the Driving Question Board after the lesson: how many GREEN notes correctly identified the Runner A / Runner B overtake as now explainable? Were there any ORANGE notes that revealed genuine new mathematical questions I had not anticipated — and if so, can I address them in Lesson 8?
5. In the Model Building phase, did students connect their new two-body diagram back to the velocity-time graph values from Lesson 6 without prompting? If students needed to be reminded to use Lesson 6 values, I need to build a stronger explicit cross-lesson reference at the START of Lesson 8 before the final synthesis task begins.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed (through calculation) that a matatu travelling at 90 km/h approaches a bus travelling in the same direction at 60 km/h at a closing speed of only 30 km/h — meaning the overtake takes much longer than the driver expects. We also observed that two Lake Victoria ferries travelling towards each other close the gap between them at 40 km/h (the SUM of their speeds), and that Runner A appeared to approach Runner B at just 4 km/h in the final sprint — the DIFFERENCE of their velocities.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that RELATIVE SPEED is the speed of one body as observed from another moving body. When two bodies move in the SAME direction, relative speed = faster speed − slower speed (they approach each other slowly). When two bodies move in OPPOSITE directions, relative speed = speed A + speed B (they approach each other rapidly). We can use relative speed to calculate the time for two bodies to meet or for one to overtake the other, using the formula: time = gap distance ÷ relative speed.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: This explains a crucial part of the marathon phenomenon: Runner A did not need to run faster than Runner B's top speed to overtake him — Runner A only needed to run faster than Runner B's CURRENT speed. Because Runner B had slowed to 17 km/h and Runner A was running at 21 km/h, the relative speed between them was 4 km/h. At that closing rate, Runner A covered the 200 m gap in approximately 3 minutes. The same mathematics also explains the NTSA road-safety context: a head-on collision between two vehicles both doing 80 km/h has a relative speed of 160 km/h — four times more dangerous than a rear-end collision between a 90 km/h matatu and a 60 km/h bus. Mathematics does not just describe motion — it saves lives.
