LESSONS.title: Consolidation, Model Building & Final Explanation: The Full Story of the Nairobi Marathon

slo.purpose: To consolidate all learning in Sub-Strand 2.9 by producing a complete mathematical explanation of the Nairobi Marathon phenomenon — integrating calculations of speed, velocity and acceleration with displacement-time and velocity-time graphs — and to demonstrate this understanding through group model presentations, DQB closure, and a class written assessment.
slo.knowledge: Learners demonstrate knowledge of: distance, displacement, speed, velocity, acceleration and relative speed; the construction and interpretation of displacement-time graphs (gradient = velocity, shape = story of motion); the construction and interpretation of velocity-time graphs (gradient = acceleration, area = displacement); and the distinction between average speed and instantaneous velocity across a 42 km race.
slo.skills: Learners accurately calculate average speed, instantaneous velocity, and acceleration from split-time tables; plot and annotate displacement-time and velocity-time graphs for two runners on the same axes; interpret graph shapes (steepness, curvature, horizontal segments) to narrate motion; compare models built in Lesson 1 with final models to show conceptual growth; communicate mathematical reasoning in written and oral form.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate the power of mathematics to reveal stories hidden in data; value integrity in accurate data recording and graph plotting; demonstrate unity by collaborating in group model presentations; show responsibility by completing the written assessment independently and honestly; and appreciate how linear motion mathematics connects to careers and everyday Kenyan life.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. What is speed? 2. How do we use displacement-time graphs in real life? 3. How do we use velocity-time graphs?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the final lesson of the storyline. Learners return to the original Nairobi Marathon split-time data that launched the driving question in Lesson 1. Armed with all the mathematical tools built across Lessons 1–7, they now produce a complete, evidence-based explanation of why Runner A won despite Runner B leading at the 30 km mark — using precise calculations, dual-runner graphs, and written interpretation of the critical sprint finish. Groups present their final models, the class closes every question on the Driving Question Board, and a written assessment consolidates all sub-strand outcomes. The lesson ends with learners reflecting on careers that use linear motion mathematics, anchoring the mathematics in the real world of Kenyan work and industry.
slo.safetyNotes: No physical hazards in this lesson. Learners should handle graph paper, rulers and calculators with care. Ensure equitable group participation — monitor that quieter learners are not sidelined during group presentations. During the written assessment, enforce a calm, respectful environment so all learners can demonstrate their individual best.

LESSONS.overview: Lesson 8 is the culminating lesson of Sub-Strand 2.9: Linear Motion. The lesson opens by returning dramatically to the 2023 Nairobi Marathon video clip and printed split-time table that launched the unit — asking learners: 'You now have all the tools. Can you finally explain exactly what happened at every kilometre of that race?' In the Predict phase, learners compare their current mental model to their Lesson 1 prediction and articulate what they now know. In the Observe phase, groups receive the full Runner A and Runner B split-time data and produce a complete mathematical portfolio: average speed calculations, segment-by-segment velocity, acceleration at the sprint finish, a dual displacement-time graph, and a dual velocity-time graph plotted on the same axes. In the Explain phase, each group presents their model to the class — teacher facilitates cross-group critique and connects every interpretation back to the phenomenon. The DQB Creation phase closes all three KICD key inquiry questions with class-agreed, evidence-based answers drawn directly from the marathon data. The Model Building phase places learners' Lesson 1 sketch beside their final graph, making conceptual growth visible. A 20-minute class written assessment covers all sub-strand SLOs. The lesson closes with a structured career reflection: learners brainstorm and discuss Kenyan careers — civil engineer designing Thika Superhighway, NTSA road safety analyst, track and field coach at Kipchoge Keino Stadium, Kenya Railways planner — that depend on the mathematics of linear motion.

framework.phase: Phase 1 — Predict: Return to the Starting Line
framework.learnerExperience: Learners view the opening 90 seconds of the Nairobi Marathon video clip again — the same clip from Lesson 1. They then receive back their original Lesson 1 prediction sheet (kept by the teacher) showing what they wrote about Runner A and Runner B before instruction began. Working individually for 3 minutes, learners write a 'Then vs. Now' comparison: (1) What did I think was happening in Lesson 1? (2) What do I know now that I did not know then? (3) In one sentence, what is my complete explanation of why Runner A won? Learners then share their 'Then vs. Now' with a shoulder partner for 2 minutes before two or three are cold-called to share with the class. This activates prior knowledge, surfaces conceptual growth, and creates emotional investment in the final explanation task.
framework.teacherMoves: Teacher replays the marathon clip on the projector and says: 'This is exactly where we started eight lessons ago. You had a puzzle — same distance, different stories, Runner B was winning at 30 km but Runner A crossed the finish line first. Look at what you wrote in Lesson 1.' Distribute Lesson 1 prediction sheets. Set a 3-minute silent individual writing timer. After 3 minutes, say: 'Turn to your shoulder partner. Share your Then vs. Now. You have 2 minutes.' WAIT for full 2 minutes. After pairs share, cold-call exactly 3 learners using a name stick: 'Tell us in one sentence — why did Runner A win?' After each response, probe with: 'How do you know that mathematically?' Record the three responses on the board under the heading 'Our Current Best Explanation.' Do NOT confirm or correct yet — hold the tension for the Observe phase. Estimated time: 10 minutes.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) Activation with 'Then vs. Now' Comparison. By physically holding their Lesson 1 prediction and comparing it to current understanding, learners make their own conceptual growth visible and concrete. This metacognitive move (recognising 'I used to think… now I think…') is a powerful sensemaking strategy that motivates the final explanation task and frames the entire lesson as the resolution of a journey.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher listens to the three cold-called responses and checks: (a) Does the learner reference velocity rather than just speed? (b) Does the learner mention the sprint finish or changing rate? (c) Does the learner use the word 'graph' or 'gradient'? Responses that remain at 'Runner A was faster' (without qualification) signal that the learner has not yet distinguished average speed from instantaneous velocity — the teacher notes these learners for targeted support during the Observe phase group work.

framework.phase: Phase 2 — Observe: Building the Complete Mathematical Portfolio
framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in pre-assigned groups of four. Each group receives: (1) the complete Runner A and Runner B split-time data table (time in minutes recorded at 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, and 42 km marks); (2) a large sheet of graph paper (A3); (3) a structured portfolio task sheet with four required outputs. Task 1 — Calculations: Compute the average speed for the whole race for both runners (km/h). Then compute the average velocity for each 5 km segment. Identify the segment where Runner B decelerates most sharply (between 25–35 km) and compute the acceleration. Task 2 — Displacement-Time Graph: Plot both runners on the same axes (time on x-axis in minutes, displacement on y-axis in km). Use different colours. Annotate: the point where Runner B is ahead (at 30 km), the sprint finish zone (40–42 km), and where the lines cross (Runner A overtakes). Task 3 — Velocity-Time Graph: Using segment velocities computed in Task 1, construct a velocity-time graph for both runners on the same axes. Annotate: Runner B's deceleration zone, Runner A's consistent gradient, and the sprint finish. Task 4 — Written Explanation: In 5–7 sentences, explain in mathematical language why Runner A won, referencing gradient, velocity, and acceleration. Groups have 25 minutes for all four tasks. The teacher circulates actively.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute materials. Read the task aloud once. Say: 'You have 25 minutes. Every member of the group must be able to explain any part of this portfolio — I will cold-call individuals, not groups, when you present.' Set a visible timer. Circulate and use targeted prompts: For Task 1 — 'What does a steeper gradient on a displacement-time graph tell you about velocity? Show me where that is in your data.' WAIT 12 seconds after asking. For Task 2 — 'Use a ruler. The gradient of each segment IS the velocity. Check: does your graph's steepness match the velocities you calculated?' For Task 3 — 'Where is Runner B's velocity going down? What does that look like on a velocity-time graph?' For Task 4 — 'Avoid saying faster or slower. Use the words gradient, velocity, and acceleration.' If a group finishes early, challenge: 'Calculate the area under Runner A's velocity-time graph for the first 20 km. What does that area represent?' Spend no more than 3 minutes with any single group. Call a 5-minute warning. Estimated time: 27 minutes (2 min setup + 25 min group work).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Mathematics Portfolio as Evidence Synthesis. Rather than a single task, the portfolio forces learners to move iteratively between numerical data (Task 1), graphical representations (Tasks 2 and 3), and verbal explanation (Task 4). This multi-representational approach — numbers → graphs → words — mirrors the practice of professional mathematicians and scientists and builds robust understanding by requiring learners to translate across modes. Each translation acts as a self-check: if the graph does not match the calculation, something is wrong and must be reconciled.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher uses a mental checklist during circulation: (a) Are displacement-time graphs plotted with correctly scaled axes and labelled units? (b) Are segment velocities correctly calculated (change in displacement ÷ change in time)? (c) Does the velocity-time graph show Runner B's velocity dropping in the 25–35 km segment and spiking for the sprint? (d) Does the written explanation include the word 'gradient' and a reference to acceleration? Groups that cannot connect the gradient of the displacement-time graph to velocity receive a targeted prompt card: 'Gradient = rise ÷ run = Δdisplacement ÷ Δtime = velocity. Apply this to your graph now.' Teacher identifies the group with the most precise Task 4 explanation to present first.

framework.phase: Phase 3 — Explain: Group Presentations and Cross-Group Critique
framework.learnerExperience: Each group has 3 minutes to present their portfolio to the class. One member holds up the A3 graph; another reads the written explanation; a third fields questions. Groups post their A3 graphs on the classroom wall (gallery style) after presenting. After all groups present, learners do a 3-minute silent 'gallery walk' — they move to look at the other groups' graphs on the wall and place a sticky dot next to the feature they find most clearly explained. The class then reconvenes and the teacher facilitates a 5-minute whole-class discussion using the gallery walk observations to identify: (1) the single clearest displacement-time graph, (2) the single clearest velocity-time graph, and (3) the single most precise written explanation. These three exemplars are used to build the class consensus final explanation on the board.
framework.teacherMoves: Announce: 'Each group has exactly 3 minutes. I will time you. After your presentation, post your graph on the wall.' Use a stopwatch strictly. After each presentation, cold-call one individual from the audience (not the presenting group): 'In one sentence, what is the most important thing that group's graph showed you?' WAIT 10 seconds. After all presentations and the gallery walk, stand at the board and say: 'Let's build one final class explanation together. I need three volunteers — one to describe the displacement-time graph, one to describe the velocity-time graph, and one to explain the sprint finish in terms of acceleration.' Write their contributions verbatim, then refine together as a class. Final board statement should read approximately: 'Runner A maintained a nearly constant velocity of approximately X km/h throughout the race. Runner B's velocity decreased significantly between km 25 and km 35, shown by the shallower gradient on the displacement-time graph and the negative slope on the velocity-time graph. In the final 2 km sprint, Runner B's velocity increased (positive acceleration) but it was insufficient to overcome the time deficit. Runner A's total time was lower because of consistent velocity, not a faster sprint.' Estimated time: 18 minutes (3 groups × 3 min + 1 min transition each = ~12 min; gallery walk = 3 min; discussion = 5 min — adjust group count as needed).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Gallery Walk with Sticky Dot Critique and Class Consensus Construction. The gallery walk externalises every group's thinking simultaneously, allowing learners to compare representations side-by-side. Peer critique (sticky dots on the clearest features) develops evaluative reasoning. Constructing the final class explanation verbally and then in writing on the board models the scientific practice of argumentation from evidence (NGSS SEP 7: Engaging in Argument from Evidence), grounding the argument in the marathon data.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher listens for precision in the three cold-called audience responses after each presentation. Key indicators: (a) Learner uses 'gradient' rather than 'steepness' when describing the graph. (b) Learner references a specific km segment rather than 'the middle of the race.' (c) Learner connects the velocity-time graph area to displacement. Vague responses ('Runner B slowed down') are probed: 'How does the graph show that? Point to the specific feature.' The class consensus statement on the board becomes a reference for the assessment phase.

framework.phase: Phase 4 — Driving Question Board (DQB) Closure: Answering Every Question
framework.learnerExperience: The full Driving Question Board — which has been built up across all 8 lessons — is displayed at the front of the class. The board shows the original driving question, all three KICD key inquiry questions, and every sticky-note question added by learners across the unit. Working as a whole class, learners now formally close each question. The teacher reads each sticky note aloud. For the three KICD key inquiry questions, the class agrees on a final answer — drawn from the marathon evidence — and the teacher writes it in a coloured marker on a card placed next to that question. For any unanswered sticky-note questions ('What happens when two runners run in opposite directions?' / 'What does deceleration look like on a velocity-time graph?'), learners vote: (a) 'We answered this — where?' or (b) 'This is a question for further study.' Unanswered questions are circled in a different colour. The driving question itself is answered last, with the full class reciting the consensus explanation built in Phase 3.
framework.teacherMoves: Stand at the DQB and say: 'Eight lessons ago, you asked how we can use mathematics to explain the motion of any moving body. Today you are going to answer that question with evidence.' Read the first KICD question: 'What is speed?' Ask: 'Someone give me our final, mathematically precise answer — using the marathon data.' WAIT 12 seconds. Cold-call. Write the answer on a green card and pin it. Repeat for questions 2 and 3. For sticky-note questions, move quickly — read each, ask for a show of hands: 'Answered — yes or no?' Mark accordingly. For the driving question, say: 'Everyone, together, say our final answer.' Lead the class in a choral recitation of the consensus explanation. Then step back and say: 'Look at this board. Every question you ever had about linear motion in this unit is answered or deliberately saved for the next level. That is what mathematicians do.' Estimated time: 8 minutes.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board Closure as Metacognitive Summary. Revisiting every question on the DQB and formally marking it 'answered' or 'for further study' gives learners a concrete, visual record of their intellectual journey. This practice mirrors the scientific community's norms of knowledge-building and revision. It also validates learner curiosity — every sticky note is taken seriously — and models that unanswered questions are not failures but invitations to further inquiry (NGSS SEP 1: Asking Questions and Defining Problems).
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher notes which questions learners mark as 'unanswered' even though they have been addressed in prior lessons — this reveals residual misconceptions. Particular attention to: (a) 'Is velocity the same as speed?' — if learners are uncertain, the teacher clarifies verbally before the assessment: 'Velocity includes direction; speed does not. A runner going back to collect a water bottle has negative velocity on our displacement-time graph.' (b) 'What does the area under a velocity-time graph mean?' — if uncertain, teacher points to the graph on the wall and traces the area with a finger.

framework.phase: Phase 5 — Model Building & Written Assessment: From Lesson 1 Sketch to Final Mathematical Model
framework.learnerExperience: Part A — Model Comparison (5 minutes): Learners place their Lesson 1 rough sketch (of what they thought Runner A and Runner B's motion looked like) beside their final, fully labelled, dual-runner displacement-time graph from today. On a reflection slip, they complete two sentences: 'In Lesson 1, my model showed… because I thought…' and 'My final model now shows… because the mathematics tells us…' These slips are collected as a formative artefact. Part B — Written Assessment (20 minutes): Learners complete an individual written assessment covering all sub-strand SLOs. Questions include: (Q1) Define velocity and distinguish it from speed, giving an example from the Nairobi Marathon. (Q2) A matatu travels from Nakuru to Naivasha (90 km) in 1.5 hours, stops for 10 minutes, then travels 60 km to Nairobi in 45 minutes. Draw the displacement-time graph and calculate the average speed for the entire journey. (Q3) From the velocity-time graph provided, calculate the acceleration in the first 10 minutes and find the total displacement for the 40-minute journey. (Q4) Two matatus leave Kisumu and Eldoret simultaneously, travelling toward each other at 80 km/h and 60 km/h respectively. The distance between the two towns is 280 km. At what time do they meet, and how far from Kisumu? (Q5) Interpret the shape of Runner B's displacement-time graph between km 25 and km 35: what does the shallower gradient tell you about Runner B's motion? Part C — Career Reflection (5 minutes, post-assessment): Learners brainstorm on a class chart: 'Which Kenyan careers use linear motion mathematics every day?' Teacher scribes responses — NTSA road safety analyst, Kenya Railways planner, civil engineer on the Nairobi Expressway, athletics coach at Kipchoge Keino Stadium in Eldoret, SGR locomotive driver, Nairobi Marathon race director. Teacher closes: 'Every career on this list needs exactly what you built in this unit — the ability to read, draw, and explain motion using numbers and graphs.'
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute Lesson 1 sketches and reflection slips. Say: 'You have 5 minutes. Place your Lesson 1 sketch and your final graph side by side. Complete the two sentences on your reflection slip. Be honest — growth in understanding is what we celebrate here.' Collect slips after 5 minutes. Distribute assessment papers. Say clearly: 'This is individual work. No group discussion. You have exactly 20 minutes. Use the class consensus explanation on the board as a reminder of your mathematical vocabulary — but all working must be your own.' Set a timer. Circulate silently, noting learners who appear stuck on Q2 (common error: forgetting to include the stationary period on the graph). Do not give answers but may prompt: 'Read the question again. How many stages does this journey have?' With 5 minutes remaining, give a verbal warning. Collect all papers. Open the career reflection chart and ask: 'Shout out a Kenyan career that uses what you learned.' Scribe rapidly for 3 minutes. Close with: 'The Nairobi Marathon runners and the matatu drivers on the Nakuru highway do not know they are living inside a mathematics lesson — but you do. That is the power of what you have learned.' Estimated time: 5 min model comparison + 20 min assessment + 5 min careers = 30 minutes.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model Comparison as Visible Learning Growth (Lesson 1 vs. Final Model). Placing the naive Lesson 1 sketch beside the final mathematically rigorous dual-runner graph makes conceptual change physically visible to each learner. This is a powerful metacognitive sensemaking strategy: learners see not just what they now know, but how their thinking changed and why — because the evidence from the marathon data demanded it. The written assessment then provides individual accountability for the knowledge, skills and attitudes developed across the unit. The career reflection anchors the mathematics in authentic Kenyan professional contexts, fulfilling the KICD value of connecting education to the world of work (NGSS SEP 8: Obtaining, Evaluating and Communicating Information).
framework.formativeAssessment: Reflection slips are collected and reviewed: teacher checks whether the 'final model' sentence includes at least one mathematical term (gradient, velocity, acceleration, displacement). Written assessment Q2 and Q3 are the primary summative indicators for graph-drawing and graph-interpretation SLOs. Q4 (relative speed) tests the final sub-strand outcome. Q5 (graph interpretation in the marathon context) closes the loop on the phenomenon. Rubric levels (Exceeds / Meets / Approaches / Below Expectations) align to the KICD suggested assessment rubric for Linear Motion: Ability to determine displacement, speed, velocity, acceleration; Ability to draw and interpret graphs of linear motion; Ability to solve problems involving relative speed.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After Lesson 8, reflect on the following questions before closing the unit: (1) Phenomenon closure — Did every learner produce a written sentence that explains why Runner A won using at least two mathematical terms (e.g., velocity and gradient)? If not, which learners need individual follow-up? (2) Graph accuracy — Were the majority of dual-runner displacement-time graphs correctly scaled, labelled with units, and annotated with the overtaking point and sprint finish zone? Common errors to note for future units: forgetting units on axes, drawing straight lines where curves are appropriate (e.g., the sprint finish), and confusing the x-axis label (time) with the y-axis label (displacement). (3) DQB effectiveness — Did the sticky-note questions evolve across the 8 lessons in a way that reflected genuine conceptual growth? Were there persistent questions (e.g., 'What is the difference between speed and velocity?') that suggest the unit needs earlier, more explicit treatment? (4) Assessment data — Review Q2 (displacement-time graph with a stop) and Q4 (relative speed) as key diagnostic items. If more than 30% of learners score Below Expectations on Q4, consider adding one consolidation lesson on relative speed in the next iteration of this unit. (5) Career relevance — Did learners connect linear motion to Kenyan careers authentically, or did responses remain generic? In future, invite a guest speaker — e.g., an NTSA road safety officer or a Kenya Railways engineer — to speak to the class during this lesson's career reflection segment, making the connection between school mathematics and professional practice vivid and personal. (6) Storyline integrity — Did the return to the Nairobi Marathon phenomenon in Lesson 8 feel like a satisfying resolution of the question posed in Lesson 1, or did it feel procedural? The emotional payoff of 'now I can explain this' is pedagogically essential — if it felt flat, consider adding a brief moment where the original video is paused mid-clip and a learner narrates what is mathematically happening on screen in real time.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners re-watched the 2023 Nairobi Marathon video clip showing elite Kenyan runners — including Runner A and Runner B — with different pacing strategies. FINAL_EXPLANATION.subjectLabel: Core Mathematics – Grade 10 | Sub-Strand 2.9: Linear Motion
FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions:
This Final Explanation is your opportunity to show everything you have learned about linear motion by answering the driving question fully and completely. You will use mathematics — both calculations and graphs — to tell the complete story of motion, just like a sports analyst breaking down a Nairobi Marathon race.

READ THE DRIVING QUESTION CAREFULLY BEFORE YOU BEGIN:
"How can we use mathematics — calculations and graphs — to fully describe and explain the motion of any moving body, from a Nairobi Marathon runner to a matatu on the Nakuru highway?"

YOUR TASK: Write a detailed, structured explanation that answers the driving question. Your response must include all four sections below. For each section, write in full sentences, show all working for any calculations, and draw or describe graphs clearly with labelled axes, units, and key features. Use specific values and examples — do not give vague or general answers.

BEFORE YOU WRITE, ask yourself:
• Can I explain the difference between distance and displacement, speed and velocity?
• Can I calculate average speed, average velocity, and read instantaneous values from a graph?
• Can I sketch AND interpret both a displacement-time graph and a velocity-time graph?
• Can I explain what the shape of each graph tells us — not just the start and end points?
• Can I connect every idea back to a real moving body (the marathon runners, a matatu, an athlete)?

You have 60 minutes. Write directly in the spaces provided under each section.

sections.title: Section 1 — The Language of Motion: Key Concepts and Definitions
sections.prompt:
Define and distinguish between the following pairs of terms, using the Nairobi Marathon runners OR a matatu on the Nakuru highway as your context. For each definition, include the formula, SI units, and ONE worked numerical example using realistic values.

(a) Distance vs. Displacement
(b) Speed vs. Velocity
(c) Average speed/velocity vs. Instantaneous speed/velocity
(d) Uniform motion vs. Non-uniform motion (acceleration)

Finish this section by explaining: Why is it NOT enough to say 'Runner B covered 42 km in 2 hours 12 minutes' if you want to fully understand how Runner B moved during the race?
sections.exemplar:
EXEMPLAR RESPONSE:

(a) Distance vs. Displacement
Distance is the total length of the path travelled by a moving body, regardless of direction. It is a scalar quantity — it has magnitude only. Displacement is the straight-line distance from the starting point to the finishing point, measured in a specific direction. It is a vector quantity — it has both magnitude and direction.

Marathon context: The 2023 Nairobi Marathon course winds through Uhuru Highway, Haile Selassie Avenue, and back. Runner A travels a total distance of 42.195 km along the road. However, if the start and finish line are at the same point (as in a loop course), the displacement is 0 km. If the course is a straight out-and-back on Mombasa Road, and the finish is 10 km north of the start, displacement = 10 km north.

(b) Speed vs. Velocity
Speed = Distance ÷ Time. It is a scalar quantity (magnitude only). SI unit: metres per second (m/s).
Velocity = Displacement ÷ Time. It is a vector quantity (magnitude + direction). SI unit: m/s.

Worked example — Nakuru highway matatu:
A matatu travels 90 km from Nairobi to Nakuru in 1.5 hours, heading north-west.
Average speed = 90 km ÷ 1.5 h = 60 km/h = 16.7 m/s
Average velocity = 90 km north-west ÷ 1.5 h = 60 km/h north-west = 16.7 m/s north-west

(c) Average speed/velocity vs. Instantaneous speed/velocity
Average speed is the total distance divided by the total time for an entire journey. Instantaneous speed is the speed of a body at one specific moment in time — the value you would read on a speedometer at a single instant.

Worked example — Runner B:
Runner B's split time at the 35 km mark is 1 h 58 min, and at the 40 km mark it is 2 h 06 min.
Average speed over that 5 km segment = 5 km ÷ 8 min = 0.625 km/min = 10.4 m/s... 
[Re-calculation]: 5000 m ÷ 480 s = 10.4 m/s. This tells us Runner B's average speed in that segment, but the instantaneous velocity at exactly the 37 km mark could be higher or lower — we cannot know from the table alone. That is why we need a graph.

(d) Uniform vs. Non-uniform motion
Uniform motion: a body moves equal distances in equal time intervals — speed is constant, acceleration = 0. Runner A's middle kilometres (km 10–35) are approximately uniform.
Non-uniform motion: a body covers unequal distances in equal time intervals — speed is changing, meaning the body is accelerating or decelerating. Runner B shows non-uniform motion: fast start, slower middle, sprint finish.

Why a single total-time statement is not enough:
Saying 'Runner B covered 42 km in 2 h 12 min' gives us only one number — the overall average speed ≈ 19.2 km/h. It tells us nothing about the fact that Runner B was running at perhaps 22 km/h in the first 5 km, dropped to 17 km/h by km 25, then surged to 23 km/h in the final 2 km. The single number hides the entire story of acceleration, strategy, and the critical sprint that Runner A used to overtake Runner B. Only split-time data and graphs reveal that full story.

sections.title: Section 2 — Displacement-Time Graphs: Drawing, Reading, and Interpreting
sections.prompt:
Using the split-time data below for Runner A and Runner B, answer all parts.

SPLIT-TIME TABLE (approximate values for use in this assessment):
| Distance (km) | Runner A time (min) | Runner B time (min) |
|---------------|--------------------|--------------------||
| 0             | 0                  | 0                  |
| 5             | 22                 | 19                 |
| 10            | 44                 | 40                 |
| 15            | 66                 | 63                 |
| 20            | 88                 | 87                 |
| 25            | 110                | 113                |
| 30            | 132                | 138                |
| 35            | 154                | 163                |
| 40            | 176                | 186                |
| 42            | 185                | 196                |

(a) Sketch a displacement-time graph for BOTH runners on the same axes. Label axes with correct quantities and units. Plot all data points and draw a smooth curve through them.
(b) What does the GRADIENT (slope) of a displacement-time graph represent? State the formula and units.
(c) Calculate the average speed of Runner A and Runner B over the full 42 km. Show all working.
(d) Using the graph, identify and explain THREE specific moments or segments where the two runners' speeds were different. Refer to specific km marks and describe what the shape of each curve tells you.
(e) Runner B was ahead at km 30. Use the graph to explain precisely how and when Runner A overtook Runner B. What does the crossing of the two curves represent?
sections.exemplar:
EXEMPLAR RESPONSE:

(a) Graph Description (sketch in your booklet):
Horizontal axis (x-axis): Time in minutes, labelled 'Time (min)', scale 0 to 200 min.
Vertical axis (y-axis): Displacement in km, labelled 'Displacement (km)', scale 0 to 42 km.
Runner A: Points are nearly equally spaced in time — the curve is close to a straight line (nearly uniform gradient), indicating nearly constant speed throughout.
Runner B: The first segment (0–10 km) has a steeper gradient than Runner A — Runner B's curve rises more quickly, showing higher speed. From km 15–35, the gradient becomes shallower than Runner A — Runner B slows. From km 40–42, the gradient steepens again — the sprint finish. The two curves cross between km 30 and km 35.

(b) Gradient of a displacement-time graph = Velocity
Formula: gradient = Δdisplacement ÷ Δtime = (s₂ − s₁) ÷ (t₂ − t₁)
Units: km/min or m/s
A steeper gradient → higher velocity. A shallower gradient → lower velocity. A horizontal line → the body is stationary (velocity = 0). A straight line → uniform velocity. A curve → changing velocity (acceleration or deceleration).

(c) Average speed calculations:
Runner A: Total distance = 42 km, Total time = 185 min = 185 ÷ 60 h = 3.083 h
Average speed = 42 ÷ 3.083 = 13.62 km/h = 13620 m ÷ 11100 s = 3.78 m/s ✓

Runner B: Total distance = 42 km, Total time = 196 min = 3.267 h
Average speed = 42 ÷ 3.267 = 12.86 km/h = 3.57 m/s ✓

Runner A's average speed is higher — confirming Runner A won, despite being behind at km 30.

(d) Three key differences identified from the graph:

① km 0–10 (time 0–40 min for A, 0–40 min for B):
Runner B's curve has a noticeably steeper gradient in the first 5 km (Runner B reaches km 5 at 19 min vs Runner A at 22 min). Runner B was running faster — approximately 5 km ÷ 19 min = 0.263 km/min = 15.8 km/h compared to Runner A's 5 km ÷ 22 min = 13.6 km/h. Runner B's fast start is clear from the curve being above and to the left of Runner A's.

② km 20–35 (the middle section):
Here Runner B's gradient becomes shallower than Runner A's — Runner B's curve flattens relative to Runner A's. For example, km 25–30: Runner B takes 138 − 113 = 25 min for 5 km → speed = 5 ÷ 25 = 0.20 km/min = 12 km/h. Runner A takes 132 − 110 = 22 min for 5 km → speed = 5 ÷ 22 = 0.227 km/min = 13.6 km/h. Runner A is pulling ahead in speed, even though Runner B is still ahead in position at this point.

③ km 40–42 (the sprint finish):
Runner B's gradient steepens sharply again — Runner B sprints. Runner B covers the last 2 km in 196 − 186 = 10 min → speed = 2 ÷ 10 = 0.2 km/min = 12 km/h. But Runner A covers it in 185 − 176 = 9 min → speed = 2 ÷ 9 = 0.222 km/min = 13.3 km/h. Runner A's sprint is slightly stronger — and crucially, Runner A had already overtaken Runner B.

(e) The crossing point:
On the graph, the two curves cross somewhere between km 30 and km 35. At km 30, Runner B is at position 30 km but has used 138 min; Runner A is also at 30 km but has used only 132 min — meaning Runner A passed the 30 km mark 6 minutes EARLIER. So although Runner B's displacement line is above Runner A's when you look at position at the same time, by km 30 Runner A is ahead in TIME. 

The correct interpretation: if you read the graph horizontally (at a fixed time, say t = 132 min), Runner A is at km 30 while Runner B has not yet reached km 30. Runner A is ahead. The crossing point on the graph (where both runners have the same displacement at the same time) occurred earlier — around km 22–25 — which is the exact moment Runner A overtook Runner B. After that point, Runner A's curve is always above Runner B's curve, meaning Runner A is always further along the course at any given time. This is exactly the power of a displacement-time graph: it shows you not just where each runner finished, but every moment of relative position throughout the race.

sections.title: Section 3 — Velocity-Time Graphs: Drawing, Reading, and Calculating Area
sections.prompt:
Use the speed values you calculated in Section 2 (one speed value per 5 km segment for each runner) to answer the following.

(a) Sketch a velocity-time graph for BOTH runners on the same axes. Plot the average speed for each 5 km segment at the midpoint time of that segment. Label all axes with correct quantities and units.
(b) What does the GRADIENT of a velocity-time graph represent? State the formula and units. Is Runner A accelerating or decelerating in any segment? What about Runner B?
(c) What does the AREA under a velocity-time graph represent? State the formula and units.
(d) Shade and calculate the area under Runner A's velocity-time graph for the first 30 km. Explain what this area represents physically.
(e) A matatu on the Nakuru highway accelerates uniformly from rest to 80 km/h in 20 seconds, travels at constant 80 km/h for 5 minutes, then brakes uniformly to a stop in 15 seconds. Sketch the velocity-time graph and calculate: (i) the acceleration during the first phase, (ii) the deceleration during the braking phase, (iii) the total distance travelled.
sections.exemplar:
EXEMPLAR RESPONSE:

(a) Velocity-time graph description:
Horizontal axis: Time (min), from 0 to 200 min.
Vertical axis: Speed (km/min) or (km/h), from 0 upward.

Approximate segment speeds for each runner (km/min), using Δdistance ÷ Δtime:
Runner A: Each segment ≈ 5 km ÷ 22 min ≈ 0.227 km/min — nearly constant across all segments → the velocity-time graph is nearly a horizontal straight line.
Runner B: Segment 1 (0–5 km): 5÷19 = 0.263 km/min; Segment 2 (5–10): 5÷21 = 0.238; Segment 3 (10–15): 5÷23 = 0.217; Segment 4 (15–20): 5÷24 = 0.208; Segment 5 (20–25): 5÷26 = 0.192; Segment 6 (25–30): 5÷25 = 0.200; Segment 7 (30–35): 5÷25 = 0.200; Segment 8 (35–40): 5÷23 = 0.217; Segment 9 (40–42): 2÷10 = 0.200 km/min.
Runner B's graph: starts high, curves downward to a minimum around km 20–25, then rises slightly for the sprint — a U-shaped or 'swooping' pattern.

(b) Gradient of a velocity-time graph = Acceleration
Formula: a = Δv ÷ Δt (change in velocity divided by change in time)
Units: km/min² or m/s²

Runner A: The velocity is nearly constant across all segments → gradient ≈ 0 → acceleration ≈ 0. Runner A runs at nearly uniform velocity. This matches the nearly straight displacement-time graph from Section 2.
Runner B: From segment 1 to segment 5, velocity decreases → negative gradient → Runner B is decelerating (slowing down). From segment 7 to segment 8, velocity increases slightly → positive gradient → Runner B is accelerating (the sprint finish). The largest deceleration is in the early-to-middle transition.

(c) Area under a velocity-time graph = Distance (displacement) travelled
Formula: Area = velocity × time (for uniform velocity rectangles) or ½ × base × height (for triangular acceleration/deceleration phases)
Units: km/min × min = km, or m/s × s = m

(d) Area under Runner A's graph for the first 30 km:
Runner A's average speed ≈ 0.227 km/min (nearly constant).
Time to reach km 30 = 132 min.
Area = speed × time = 0.227 km/min × 132 min = 29.96 km ≈ 30 km ✓
Physical meaning: This area represents the total distance Runner A has covered in the first 132 minutes of the race — exactly 30 km. This confirms that the area under a velocity-time graph gives us displacement, linking directly back to the displacement-time graph. The fact that we recover 30 km from the area calculation validates our graph and our understanding of the relationship between the two graph types.

(e) Nakuru highway matatu — three-phase journey:

Phase 1 — Acceleration from rest to 80 km/h in 20 s:
Convert: 80 km/h = 80 × 1000 ÷ 3600 = 22.22 m/s; initial velocity u = 0 m/s.
(i) Acceleration = Δv ÷ Δt = (22.22 − 0) ÷ 20 = 1.11 m/s² ✓
Distance in Phase 1 = area of triangle = ½ × 20 s × 22.22 m/s = 222.2 m

Phase 2 — Constant 80 km/h = 22.22 m/s for 5 minutes = 300 s:
Distance = 22.22 × 300 = 6666 m = 6.67 km

Phase 3 — Braking from 22.22 m/s to rest in 15 s:
(ii) Deceleration = Δv ÷ Δt = (0 − 22.22) ÷ 15 = −1.48 m/s² (magnitude: 1.48 m/s²) ✓
Distance in Phase 3 = area of triangle = ½ × 15 s × 22.22 m/s = 166.7 m

(iii) Total distance = 222.2 + 6666 + 166.7 = 7054.9 m ≈ 7.05 km ✓

Velocity-time graph: starts at (0, 0), rises in a straight line to (20 s, 22.22 m/s) [Phase 1 — triangle], stays horizontal at 22.22 m/s from t = 20 s to t = 320 s [Phase 2 — rectangle], then drops in a straight line from (320 s, 22.22 m/s) to (335 s, 0) [Phase 3 — triangle]. All axes are labelled: x-axis 'Time (s)', y-axis 'Velocity (m/s)'.

sections.title: Section 4 — Answering the Driving Question: The Full Story of Motion
sections.prompt:
Now bring everything together. Write a full, connected explanation (minimum 3 paragraphs) that directly answers the driving question:

'How can we use mathematics — calculations and graphs — to fully describe and explain the motion of any moving body, from a Nairobi Marathon runner to a matatu on the Nakuru highway?'

Your answer MUST:
• Reference specific calculations you did in Sections 1–3 (use actual numbers)
• Explain the role of BOTH the displacement-time graph AND the velocity-time graph, and what each one reveals that the other does not
• Explain why average speed alone is insufficient and what instantaneous velocity adds to our understanding
• Connect back to the original puzzle: Runner B was ahead at km 30 but Runner A won — use mathematics to explain exactly how this was possible
• Generalise your answer: explain how the same mathematical tools apply to the matatu on the Nakuru highway or to any other moving body
sections.exemplar:
EXEMPLAR RESPONSE:

Mathematics gives us a precise, complete language for describing motion — one that goes far beyond simply saying 'Runner A won' or 'the matatu went fast.' In this unit, we learned that any moving body can be described using two key measurements: displacement (how far it has moved from its starting point, in a specific direction) and velocity (how quickly that displacement changes over time). By calculating average speed — for example, Runner A's average speed of 42 km ÷ 185 min = 0.227 km/min = 13.62 km/h and Runner B's 42 km ÷ 196 min = 12.86 km/h — we can confirm who covered the ground faster overall. But these two numbers alone do not explain the most interesting part of the race: how Runner B was ahead at km 30 and still lost. That deeper explanation requires graphs.

The displacement-time graph tells the story of WHERE each body is at every moment in time. When we plotted both runners on the same axes, the graph revealed something that the split-time table only hinted at: Runner B's curve was higher (further along the course) than Runner A's curve in the early stages, but the gradient of Runner B's curve — which represents velocity — gradually became shallower from km 15 onwards, meaning Runner B was slowing down. Runner A's nearly straight-line curve maintained a consistent gradient of approximately 0.227 km/min throughout. The exact moment the two curves crossed — around km 22–25 — is the precise instant Runner A overtook Runner B. After that crossing point, Runner A's curve is always above Runner B's, meaning Runner A was always further ahead. No single average-speed calculation could show us this crossing point; only the graph reveals it. This is the fundamental power of a displacement-time graph: the shape of the curve carries information that numbers alone cannot.

The velocity-time graph adds a second layer of understanding by showing HOW FAST each body is moving at every moment, and whether it is accelerating or decelerating. For Runner B, the velocity-time graph showed a high starting speed (~0.263 km/min), a declining curve through the middle of the race (reaching a minimum near km 20–25), and a slight upturn for the sprint finish. The gradient of this curve is acceleration — Runner B's negative gradient in the middle confirmed deceleration; the positive gradient near the end confirmed the sprint acceleration. The area under the velocity-time curve confirmed our displacement calculations: for Runner A, the area (speed × time) over 132 minutes correctly recovered approximately 30 km — physically, the area represents the total distance covered. These same tools apply universally: for the Nakuru highway matatu that accelerated from 0 to 22.22 m/s in 20 seconds (acceleration = 1.11 m/s²), cruised for 5 minutes, then braked to rest in 15 seconds (deceleration = 1.48 m/s²), the velocity-time graph gave us the total journey distance of 7.05 km from pure area calculations — no ruler needed on the road. Whether the moving body is an elite Kenyan marathon runner, a matatu, a cyclist in Kisumu, or a ball rolling down a hill in the Rift Valley, the same displacement-time and velocity-time graphs, the same gradient and area calculations, and the same distinction between average and instantaneous velocity give us the complete, precise, and beautiful mathematical description of motion.

SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: How can we use mathematics — calculations and graphs — to fully describe and explain the motion of any moving body, from a Nairobi Marathon runner to a matatu on the Nakuru highway?

lessons.title: Anchoring Phenomenon & Key Terms: What Is Really Happening in the Nairobi Marathon?
lessons.observed: Learners examined a simplified race report of a Nairobi Marathon runner — including split times, route map segments, and a finish-line photo — and discussed what they noticed and wondered about the runner's journey. They compared the total road distance run (42.195 km of winding Nairobi streets) with the straight-line displacement from Nyayo Stadium start to finish, observing that the two values are not equal.
lessons.learned: Distance is the total path length covered, measured in metres or kilometres, and is a scalar quantity — direction is not required. Displacement is the straight-line change in position from start to end point, measured in the same units but also requiring a stated direction, making it a vector quantity. Speed is the rate of change of distance (distance ÷ time); velocity is the rate of change of displacement (displacement ÷ time) and also requires direction. These four terms are the foundational vocabulary for all subsequent lessons.
lessons.explained: The Nairobi Marathon runner covers more distance than their displacement because the road curves — total tarmac underfoot ≠ straight-line gap between start and finish. Pedagogical note: stress early that confusing 'distance' and 'displacement' is the single most common error in this sub-strand. Use a physical demonstration — walk a curved path around desks, then stretch a string straight back — to make the distinction concrete before any calculation is attempted. Cold-call at least four learners to state a definition in their own words before moving on.

lessons.title: Calculating Speed, Velocity & Time: Putting Numbers to the Race
lessons.observed: Learners were given a structured data table containing split distances and split times for three fictional runners in the Nairobi Marathon (Runner A — Eliud from Eldoret, Runner B — Amina from Mombasa, Runner C — Otieno from Kisumu). They performed calculations for each segment: average speed = distance ÷ time, average velocity = displacement ÷ time, and rearranged the formula to find missing distance or time values. A matatu scenario on the Nakuru highway was introduced as a parallel context.
lessons.learned: The mathematical relationships speed = distance/time, velocity = displacement/time, distance = speed × time, and time = distance/speed can be rearranged and applied to solve for any one unknown given the other two. Average speed and instantaneous speed are distinguished: average speed covers the whole journey; instantaneous speed is the speed at one particular moment. Units must be consistent — convert km/h to m/s by dividing by 3.6 (or multiplying by 5/18).
lessons.explained: Runner A may have a higher average speed over the first 10 km than Runner B, yet Runner B finishes faster overall — demonstrating that a single-segment calculation cannot describe an entire journey. Pedagogical note: insist learners write the formula, substitute values with units, and write a concluding statement with units in every worked example. A common error is dividing time by distance instead of the reverse — build a 'formula triangle' anchor chart for the classroom wall. Provide at least two km/h ↔ m/s conversion practice items before the matatu problem.

lessons.title: Drawing Displacement-Time Graphs: Reading the Shape of the Race
lessons.observed: Learners plotted displacement-time (s-t) graphs for Eliud's marathon segments using pre-prepared data tables, choosing appropriate scales and labelling axes correctly. They then compared their graphs with a teacher-drawn reference graph projected on the board, identifying where the line was steep, gentle, horizontal, or sloping downward.
lessons.learned: The shape of a displacement-time graph tells the full story of motion: a steep positive line indicates high speed in the positive direction; a gentle positive line indicates low speed; a horizontal line (zero gradient) means the object is stationary; a negative slope means the object is moving back toward the origin. The graph is a visual narrative — each segment's shape corresponds directly to a phase of the journey.
lessons.explained: Eliud's s-t graph rises steeply in the early kilometres (fresh legs, downhill from Uhuru Highway), flattens slightly on the return loop (fatigue, uphill), and continues to rise to the finish — the varying steepness encodes the changing pace. Pedagogical note: before learners plot, spend 3 minutes on axis-scaling decisions — a poorly scaled graph is the most frequent source of error. Ask learners to describe each segment in plain English BEFORE they attempt to calculate gradients, so graph-reading precedes gradient arithmetic. This lesson is the bridge between numerical and graphical representations.

lessons.title: Interpreting Displacement-Time Graphs: Gradient as Velocity
lessons.observed: Learners calculated the gradient of each straight-line segment on their previously drawn s-t graphs using gradient = rise ÷ run = Δs ÷ Δt, then compared the calculated gradient values to the velocity values computed numerically in Lesson 2. They also examined a provided graph of the Nakuru matatu journey and identified stationary periods, high-speed segments, and direction reversals.
lessons.learned: The gradient of a displacement-time graph is numerically equal to the velocity of the object during that segment. A zero gradient equals zero velocity (object is stationary). A negative gradient equals motion in the negative direction (back toward or past the start). A steeper gradient equals greater speed. This is the key quantitative link between the graphical and numerical representations.
lessons.explained: Learners can now extract a velocity value directly from a graph without a separate data table — the graph itself is a calculation tool. Pedagogical note: emphasise that gradient is always calculated as vertical change ÷ horizontal change (Δy ÷ Δx), never the reverse. A persistent misconception is that a 'steeper' line always means 'farther from start' — clarify that steepness encodes rate, not position. Use at least two cold-call 'what is the velocity in this segment?' questions where the answer is zero or negative to surface and correct this error.

lessons.title: Introduction to Velocity-Time Graphs: Drawing the Matatu's Speed Story
lessons.observed: Learners were given a new data set describing a matatu journey from Nairobi's CBD to Nakuru: several phases including acceleration from rest at a bus stage, constant cruising speed on the open highway, deceleration into Naivasha town, a stationary stop, and further acceleration to Nakuru. Learners plotted velocity-time (v-t) graphs from this data, choosing appropriate scales and labelling axes with correct units.
lessons.learned: A velocity-time graph plots velocity (y-axis, m/s or km/h) against time (x-axis, seconds or minutes). A horizontal line means constant velocity (no acceleration). A positive slope means the object is accelerating (speeding up). A negative slope means the object is decelerating (slowing down). A line touching the x-axis means the object is at rest (v = 0). The v-t graph is a complementary tool to the s-t graph — together they give a complete picture of motion.
lessons.explained: The matatu's v-t graph rises from zero (starting from rest at the Nairobi bus stage), levels off at a constant cruise velocity on the open highway, dips to zero at the Naivasha stop, then rises again — the graph shape matches the real physical experience of the journey. Pedagogical note: many learners initially confuse the s-t and v-t graph shapes. Display both graph types side by side on the board throughout this lesson. A useful teaching move is to ask learners to physically stand up and mime acceleration (lean forward), constant speed (walk steadily), and deceleration (lean back) while describing each graph segment.

lessons.title: Interpreting Velocity-Time Graphs: Area Under the Graph as Distance
lessons.observed: Learners examined a velocity-time graph for the matatu journey and were guided to calculate: (i) the gradient of each sloped segment to find acceleration or deceleration values, and (ii) the area of each geometric shape under the graph (rectangles for constant speed, triangles for acceleration/deceleration phases) to find distance travelled in each phase.
lessons.learned: The gradient of a velocity-time graph equals acceleration: a = Δv ÷ Δt. A steep positive gradient means rapid acceleration; a negative gradient (deceleration) has a negative value. The area under a velocity-time graph equals the distance travelled during that time interval. For rectangular sections: area = base × height = time × velocity = distance. For triangular sections (acceleration/deceleration): area = ½ × base × height = ½ × time × Δv = distance. The unit check confirms this: (m/s) × s = m.
lessons.explained: The matatu's total journey distance can be recovered entirely from the v-t graph by summing all the areas under each segment — no separate distance data is needed. Pedagogical note: the area-under-the-graph concept is the most conceptually demanding idea in this sub-strand. Use colour-coded shading for each geometric region before any calculation. Insist learners label each shape (rectangle, triangle), write the area formula, substitute, and state units. A frequent error is using the full height of a trapezoid as the triangle height — decompose trapezoids into rectangle + triangle explicitly.

lessons.title: Equations of Linear Motion & Combining Graphs: Solving the Full Journey
lessons.observed: Learners were introduced to the four equations of linear motion (v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as; s = ½(u + v)t) and applied them to solve multi-step problems set in Kenyan contexts — a boda-boda accelerating from rest in Kisumu, a Rift Valley Express bus braking on the Nakuru highway, and an athlete's sprint at the Moi International Sports Centre. Learners also practised moving between graph and equation representations for the same scenario.
lessons.learned: The four kinematic equations apply to objects undergoing uniform (constant) acceleration in a straight line. Each equation links a different combination of the five variables: initial velocity (u), final velocity (v), acceleration (a), time (t), and displacement (s). The strategy for solving any problem is: (1) list known and unknown quantities with units, (2) select the equation that contains the unknown and all three known quantities, (3) substitute and solve, (4) state the answer with correct units and direction where applicable.
lessons.explained: The equations and the graphs are two languages describing the same physical reality — for example, v = u + at is the algebraic form of reading the gradient on a v-t graph, and s = ½(u + v)t is the algebraic form of calculating the trapezoid area. Pedagogical note: display the four equations permanently on the board for the remainder of the unit. A structured 'KUSD' framework (Known, Unknown, Select equation, Do the maths) reduces errors significantly. Require learners to check answers by substituting back into the original equation before writing a final answer.

lessons.title: Consolidation, Model Building & Final Explanation: The Full Story of the Nairobi Marathon
lessons.observed: Learners returned to the Nairobi Marathon anchoring phenomenon and used all tools acquired across Lessons 1–7 to produce a complete mathematical explanation of the race. They calculated average speed and velocity for each race segment, identified acceleration and deceleration phases, drew and annotated both s-t and v-t graphs for the full 42.195 km journey, computed distances from graph areas, and applied kinematic equations to answer 'what if' extension questions about the race.
lessons.learned: A moving body's complete motion can be described using: scalar quantities (distance, speed) and vector quantities (displacement, velocity, acceleration); displacement-time graphs (gradient = velocity); velocity-time graphs (gradient = acceleration, area = distance); and the four kinematic equations for uniform acceleration. These tools are complementary — numerical, graphical, and algebraic representations all encode the same underlying motion and can be used interchangeably depending on what information is given or required.
lessons.explained: The Nairobi Marathon runner's journey is now fully described mathematically: the winding road gives total distance 42.195 km; the net displacement from Nyayo Stadium start to finish line is calculable from the route map; each split segment has a calculable average velocity; acceleration and deceleration phases are visible on the v-t graph and quantifiable via kinematic equations. Pedagogical note: this lesson functions as a summative performance task. Learners should work in pairs to produce a poster or annotated graph set — assess both the mathematical accuracy and the quality of the written explanation linking calculations back to the driving question. Celebrate the journey: learners began by observing a race; they now have the full mathematical toolkit to describe any moving body.
